children.text: The Elbaf arc has dropped one of One Piece's most shocking revelations—the tragic connection between Brook and Gunko. What began as a musical obsession has unraveled into a heartbreaking tale of royalty, betrayal, and suppressed memories spanning over 50 years.
Here's everything we know about Brook and Gunko's mysterious past, including the latest Chapter 1173 manga spoilers revealing her true identity.
Who Is Brook? The Soul King's Hidden Past
Brook is the Straw Hat Pirates' musician and ninth crew member, but his journey to Luffy's side is layered with tragedy most fans don't fully appreciate.
Before the Rumbar Pirates

Born 90 years ago, Brook served as the battle convoy leader for an unnamed kingdom in the West Blue. He received formal education and developed exceptional swordsmanship alongside his musical talents. More importantly, he served directly under a king he considered his benefactor—someone who shaped his entire worldview.
During this period, Brook's life intersected with a young princess who would eventually become the Holy Knight Gunko.
The Rumbar Pirates Tragedy
About 52 years ago, Brook joined the music-themed Rumbar Pirates. They befriended Laboon, a baby Island Whale, promising to return after sailing the Grand Line.

When disease struck half the crew, Brook became captain. In the Florian Triangle, enemy pirates attacked with poisoned weapons. As crewmates slowly died, Brook recorded "Binks' Sake" on a Tone Dial—a final song for Laboon.
They died one by one while playing, each with a smile. Brook's Yomi Yomi no Mi returned his soul to his decomposed skeleton. He drifted alone for 50 years until meeting the Straw Hats.
Who Is Gunko? The Holy Knight with a Broken Past
Saint Manmayer Gunko initially appeared as another ruthless Celestial Dragon antagonist. But Eiichiro Oda has gradually revealed something far more complex.
Powers and Abilities

Gunko wields the Aro Aro no Mi (Arrow-Arrow Fruit), creating dark energy arrows that bind and control opponents. She single-handedly defeated Nami, Usopp, Jinbe, and Brook, plus critically injured Scopper Gaban, the Roger Pirates' former number three.
Her most terrifying ability isn't her own—Imu can possess her body remotely, channeling their full power including Conqueror's Haki and the mysterious "Abyss" that transforms giants into demons.
The Manmayer Family Mystery
Initially, Gunko's introduction lacked the "Saint" honorific other Celestial Dragons receive, sparking massive speculation. Volume 112 corrected this, officially naming her Saint Manmayer Gunko.

The Manmayer Family is one of the original twenty royal families who became Celestial Dragons. An unnamed Manmayer woman appeared during the God Valley Incident 38 years ago. Given Gunko's youthful appearance despite being approximately 80 years old, immortality granted by Imu seems likely.
The Connection: When Brook Met Gunko
The first hint came in Chapter 1147 when Gunko captured several Straw Hats. Her singular demand? Brook as her personal music slave.
An Obsession Rooted in Memory
Gunko was shown listening to Brook's "New World" as a ritual. When they met, her fan obsession turned violent—she wanted to enslave Brook to make music eternally.

When Brook refused, Gunko kicked him brutally but visibly felt pain in her heart. This wasn't physical discomfort—it was emotional anguish suggesting a deeper connection. Brook also seemed to recognize her but couldn't place where.
Chapter 1149: The Flashback
Truth emerged when Gunko captured Scopper Gaban and his son Colon. As Colon cried out for his father, Gunko experienced a memory breakthrough showing:
A young girl (Gunko) crying out for her father while being taken away
That girl dancing to Brook's music as he (in human form) shared his pirate dreams
This occurred over 50 years ago, before Brook joined the Rumbar Pirates. Imu immediately possessed Gunko when these memories surfaced, preventing reconnection with Brook.
Chapter 1173: Princess Shuri Revealed
The latest spoilers have revealed Gunko's true identity—and it's devastatingly tragic.
"Princess Shuri, The Father-Killing Princess"

When Brook faces Gunko directly, recognition clicks. He addresses her by her real name—Princess Shuri (or Sherry). He recognizes her blue hair, heterochromatic eyes, Holy Land connection, and love for his music.
Brook realizes if this is the same Princess Shuri, she should be 80 years old—her youthful appearance confirms Imu's immortality gift.
But Brook's next words drop the bombshell: he calls her "The Father-Killing Princess," revealing she murdered her own father—the king Brook served.
This wasn't just any king. Brook describes him as his "Onjin"—his benefactor and inspiration, mirroring what Shanks means to Luffy. The king shaped Brook's entire life and values.
The circumstances remain unclear:
Did Shuri kill her possessed father, like theories about Loki?
Was the king abusive?
Did Holy Knights orchestrate it for recruitment?
Regardless, the act destroyed Brook's world. The man he owed everything to died by the hand of the princess he may have protected. This trauma likely drove Brook to finally pursue piracy.
Gunko Fights Back
Upon hearing her true name, Gunko's consciousness breaks through Imu's control briefly. She releases Brook and the Straw Hats from her arrow restraints, desperately shouting at Brook to run.
Even as Imu forces her to attack, part of Gunko remembers who she was. This confirms Princess Shuri isn't gone—she's buried beneath brainwashing and forced servitude.
The Likely Timeline
56+ Years Ago:
Brook serves the king, bonds with Princess Shuri through music.
The Patricide:
Shuri kills her father. The kingdom falls. She's taken by Holy Knights, brainwashed, and granted immortality.
38 Years Ago:
Active during God Valley Incident.
52 Years Ago:
Devastated, Brook joins Rumbar Pirates.
Present:
Recognition after 50+ years.
Why This Revelation Matters
Brook Gets Real Development
Brook has received minimal character development since joining. The Gunko reveal gives him personal stakes in the Final Saga, finally exploring his mysterious past.
Gunko's Redemption Setup

Gunko's suppressed memories and resistance moments make her a sympathetic antagonist—a victim brainwashed for 50+ years. She may become a Straw Hat ally, continuing the pattern of redeemed antagonists.
Imu's True Power
Gunko's possession reveals Imu can fully control bodies remotely. Why her specifically remains unclear—physical resemblance to Nefertari D. Lily, immortality, or blood connection?
Holy Knights' Origins
Not all Holy Knights are born Celestial Dragons. Some are forcibly recruited and elevated, raising questions about other members' backgrounds.
Parallels and Themes
Brook's Double Promise

Both Laboon and Gunko involve promises and long separations. Brook promised to return to Laboon but was prevented by death. He may have promised to protect Princess Shuri but was prevented by patricide and departure.
Now Brook can fulfill the promise he couldn't keep—saving someone from his past.
Music as Memory

Throughout One Piece, music triggers memories and emotions. Brook's songs reached Laboon across decades. Now his music has reached through Gunko's brainwashing to touch Princess Shuri's buried consciousness.
This reinforces One Piece's core theme—bonds created through shared joy can survive even the cruelest separations.
What Happens Next?
Based on spoilers and narrative setup:

Brook will likely refuse to give up on Princess Shuri. His Laboon experience taught him that promises matter across impossible distances. Expect emotional confrontation where Brook appeals to Princess Shuri through music—the one thing breaking through conditioning.
Gunko shouting at Brook to run while possessed shows she's fighting back. This struggle will intensify, possibly culminating in her breaking free.
Luffy's arrival might be the catalyst. His ability to inspire freedom from oppression has been consistent. If anyone can help Gunko reclaim identity, it's Luffy.

If Gunko switches sides, it weakens Holy Knights and provides crucial intelligence about Imu's abilities. Her knowledge of the Holy Land, Imu's powers, and World Government inner workings could be invaluable in the coming war.
Brook's Complete Timeline
90 years ago:
Brook is born
70-65 years ago:
Becomes battle convoy leader
60-56 years ago:
Serves King, mentors Princess Shuri
56 years ago:
Princess Shuri kills her father, is taken; Brook devastated
52 years ago:
Joins Rumbar Pirates
50 years ago:
Rumbar Pirates die; Brook revives as skeleton
8 years ago:
Gecko Moria steals shadow
2 years ago:
Joins Straw Hats, becomes "Soul King"
Present:
Confronts Princess Shuri in Elbaf
This transforms Brook from comic relief into a character with one of the deepest, most tragic histories—spanning nearly a century of loss and perseverance.
The Emotional Weight
Imagine seeing someone you protected as a child transformed into a weapon serving the system that destroyed her life.

Brook already carries guilt from failing his crewmates and leaving Laboon waiting 50 years. Princess Shuri is another broken promise—but unlike dead crewmates, she's here now, still fighting to return. This gives Brook a rare chance at present redemption.
Why This Story Resonates
The Brook-Gunko storyline embodies One Piece's greatest strengths:
Long-term Storytelling:
Oda planted seeds about Brook's pre-pirate life in Thriller Bark. Over 15 years later in real time, those seeds bloom into major plot.
Moral Complexity:
Neither Brook nor Gunko is simply good or evil. Both made choices shaped by impossible circumstances. The patricide may have been justified—we don't know yet.
Emotional Depth:
This isn't just action. It's about trauma, suppressed memories, broken promises, and redemption after decades of suffering.
Thematic Consistency:
Music, memory, and the power of connections to survive separation—all core One Piece themes—weave throughout this narrative.
Conclusion: A Song Yet Unfinished

Brook's story has always been about promises and music. He promised Laboon he'd return. He promised his crew he'd deliver their final song. And somewhere, decades ago, he likely promised to protect a young princess who loved his music.
The first promise remains unfulfilled but within reach. The second was completed when he joined the Straw Hats. And now, the third—long forgotten—has suddenly resurfaced as most urgent.

Princess Shuri is still alive, buried beneath Gunko's brainwashing, crying out through brief consciousness moments. Brook has a chance to save her, to finally keep one of his promises before it's too late.

As the Elbaf arc intensifies, watch for the inevitable moment when Brook plays music for Gunko one more time—not as her captor or enemy, but as the man who once made a little princess laugh in a kingdom that no longer exists.
That song might be the key to breaking Imu's control and bringing Princess Shuri home.

After all, in One Piece, a promise is never truly broken as long as someone still remembers it. And Brook, the undead skeleton who exists only because of promises to the dying, will never stop remembering.

children.text: Mobile Suit Gundam GQuuuuuuX (pronounced "G-Quacks") is a 2025 mecha anime created by Studio Khara (Evangelion) and Sunrise that's become 2025's most viral anime. Set in an alternate Universal Century timeline where Char Aznable wins the One Year War, the 12-episode series follows high schooler Amate Yuzuriha as she pilots the GQuuuuuuX in illegal underground mecha duels. With Evangelion creator Hideaki Anno writing and FLCL director Kazuya Tsurumaki directing, it blends Gundam's political drama with experimental storytelling that's divided longtime fans but attracted newcomers. Streaming now on Prime Video.
What Is Gundam GQuuuuuuX?

Mobile Suit Gundam GQuuuuuuX is a 12-episode mecha anime that premiered in April 2025, following a theatrical compilation film in January. It's the 16th mainline Gundam installment and the first full Universal Century series since 1993's Victory Gundam—though it takes place in an alternate timeline.

The collaboration between Studio Khara (known for Neon Genesis Evangelion) and Sunrise (the legendary Gundam studio) was announced in December 2024 and immediately generated massive hype. Hideaki Anno, Yoji Enokido, and Kazuya Tsurumaki—the creative team behind Evangelion and FLCL—brought their distinctive style to the Gundam franchise.
The result? Japan's most viral anime of 2025, according to Bushiroad's Anime Data Insights Lab study of 270 series.
The Alternate Timeline That Changes Everything
In the original Mobile Suit Gundam (1979), protagonist Amuro Ray pilots the RX-78-2 White Gundam to help the Earth Federation defeat Char Aznable and the Principality of Zeon.
GQuuuuuuX flips this completely.
Here, Char steals the RX-78-2, renames it the "Red Gundam," and uses it to win Zeon's independence. Five years later, both the Red Gundam and Char have disappeared, leaving a Zeon-dominated world.
This isn't a retcon of existing Gundam continuity—it's a completely separate "what if" timeline that lets the creators explore familiar characters and conflicts from new angles.
The Story: Underground Mecha Duels and Political Conspiracy

Amate Yuzuriha is a high school student living in the Side 6 space colony Izuma. Her peaceful life shatters when she meets Nyaan, a war refugee from Side 2, and encounters Shuji, a mysterious vandal piloting the Red Gundam.
When military police brutally pursue Shuji, Amate impulsively pilots the gMS-Ω GQuuuuuuX—a next-generation mobile suit—to help him escape.
Clan Battles: Illegal Mecha Fighting

Unable to return to normal life, Amate joins "Clan Battles"—underground mobile suit duels operated by junk dealer Kaneban Co. She competes under the alias "Machu" (her childhood nickname), earning money while evading authorities.

These battles aren't just spectacle. They're how powerless people in a Zeon-controlled society create agency for themselves—fighting for survival, reputation, and connection in a world that's forgotten them.
The premise mirrors
Hajime no Ippo's competition-driven pressure
, but with giant robots and political undertones.
The Political Drama Beneath the Duels
GQuuuuuuX isn't just about mecha fights.
Beneath the Clan Battles runs a conspiracy involving Kycilia Zabi's power grab within Zeon, the mysterious "kira-kira" psychic ability Amate possesses, and Char's true motives for disappearing.
The series balances personal stakes (Amate protecting her friends) with large-scale political maneuvering, creating tension similar to
Monster's layered conspiracy approach
, though compressed into 12 episodes.
Why the Evangelion Connection Matters
The Studio Khara involvement isn't just marketing.
Hideaki Anno's Influence

Anno wrote the 30-minute prologue focusing on Char's alternate victory, filling it with the technical detail and military jargon that defined Evangelion. Characters stand in rooms delivering space opera dialogue. Mechanical systems are explained in obsessive detail.
If you've watched Evangelion, you'll immediately recognize Anno's fingerprints.
Kazuya Tsurumaki's Direction
Director Kazuya Tsurumaki (FLCL, Rebuild of Evangelion) brings rapid-fire pacing, eccentric character quirks, and kinetic action sequences that feel distinctly different from traditional Gundam.
The animation style shifts between fluid 2D hand-drawn combat and CG mobile suits, creating a visual hybrid that some fans love and others find jarring.
Ikuto Yamashita's Radical Mecha Designs
Mechanical designer Ikuto Yamashita (Evangelion, Shin Kamen Rider) reimagined classic Gundam mobile suits with angular, unsettling proportions.

The GQuuuuuuuX itself looks deliberately strange—sleek yet bulky, with articulation that challenges traditional Gundam aesthetics. Director Tsurumaki specifically told Yamashita: "I want Gunpla like nothing I've ever seen before."
The result divides fans. Some find the designs fresh and experimental. Others think they abandon what makes Gundam visually iconic.
What Makes GQuuuuuuX Different From Other Gundam Series
Shortest Mainline Gundam Ever
At just 12 episodes, GQuuuuuuX is the shortest Gundam TV series excluding OVAs.

This compressed runtime means the story moves fast—sometimes too fast. Character development that would normally unfold over 50 episodes happens in a handful of scenes. Political conspiracies that deserve explanation get rushed.
But the brevity also eliminates filler. Every episode advances the plot or deepens character relationships.
Female Protagonist in a Male-Dominated Franchise
GQuuuuuuX is only the second mainline Gundam with a female lead (after 2022's The Witch from Mercury).

Amate isn't a trained soldier or Newtype prodigy. She's an ordinary teenager thrust into piloting a Gundam by circumstance, not destiny. Her journey focuses on survival and protecting her friends rather than becoming humanity's savior.

The series explores what it calls the "female experience" of piloting Gundams—though reviews are mixed on whether it actually delivers meaningful perspective or just uses gender as surface-level differentiation.
The "Kira-Kira" Psychic Ability
Amate experiences a sensation called "kira-kira" (sparkling) that seems to enhance her piloting abilities during combat.
These sequences are visualized through surreal, almost psychedelic animation reminiscent of Evangelion's introspective scenes—reality fractures, colors shift, time feels elastic.
Whether kira-kira is a Newtype ability, something unique to Amate, or connected to the GQuuuuuuX's design remains deliberately ambiguous throughout the series.
The Reception: Viral Success, Divided Fanbase
GQuuuuuuX topped Japan's 2025 anime viral rankings in both Trend Score and Fan Score categories, beating out Sakamoto Days, Medalist, and others.
The compilation film opened at #1 at the Japanese box office in January 2025, reaching 1 million attendees in two weeks across 426 theaters (including 52 IMAX locations).
But critical and audience reception tells a more complicated story.
What Critics Praised
Animation quality:
Reviews consistently highlight the fluid combat animation and high production values. Rotten Tomatoes critics called it "some of the best robot action scenes in quite a while."
Political themes:
The series maintains Gundam's tradition of exploring war, occupation, and resistance through the lens of giant robot battles.
Accessibility for newcomers:
Unlike dense UC timeline entries, GQuuuuuuX's alternate timeline doesn't require extensive Gundam knowledge (though familiarity with the original series enhances appreciation).
What Fans Criticized
Rushed pacing:
At 12 episodes, character arcs feel compressed. Relationships that should develop organically instead happen through exposition.
Tonal inconsistency:
The series oscillates between serious political drama and arcade-style Clan Battle spectacle without always finding balance.
Underdeveloped side characters:
The show reportedly kills off one-time characters who quickly become fan favorites, leading to speculation the director didn't want to develop personalities outside the main cast.
Divisive ending:
The finale leaves major plot threads unresolved, which some viewers found honest and others found frustrating.
The Ratings Tell the Story
IMDb:
6.8/10 (across 720+ reviews)
Rotten Tomatoes (Beginning film):
90% critics, 100+ verified audience ratings
MyAnimeList:
Mixed reviews ranging from 3/10 to 10/10
The polarization is real. Evangelion fans who came for Tsurumaki's direction often loved it. Traditional Gundam fans expecting 50-episode political opera felt shortchanged.
Who Should Watch Gundam GQuuuuuuX?
Watch If You:
Want an entry point into Gundam that doesn't require watching 40+ years of continuity
Enjoyed Evangelion's experimental approach to mecha storytelling
Appreciate anime that prioritizes visual style and atmosphere, similar to
why Frieren feels different from other fantasy anime
Like short, tightly-paced series over long-running epics
Skip If You:
Prefer traditional Gundam's longer, more deliberate storytelling
Need complete narrative resolution by the finale
Dislike experimental animation styles mixing 2D and CG
Want deep character development over spectacle
Expect every plot thread to be explained
The Studio Khara Difference: Why It Feels Like Evangelion Gundam
GQuuuuuuX shares creative DNA with Evangelion in ways that go beyond superficial similarities.
The Anno Approach to Military Fiction
Both series obsess over technical detail. How mobile suits operate. What happens in command centers during battles. The protocols for launching mechas.
This isn't dry exposition—it creates immersion by treating fictional technology as if it has real operational logic.
Tsurumaki's Frenetic Energy
FLCL's hyperkinetic pacing appears in GQuuuuuuX's Clan Battle sequences. Quick cuts. Exaggerated character reactions. Action that prioritizes emotional impact over tactical realism.
This clashes with Gundam's typically grounded approach to mecha combat, creating a hybrid style that either thrills or alienates depending on your expectations.
Character Designs by Take
Illustrator Take (Katanagatari, Pokémon) created character designs that look distinctly modern compared to classic Gundam's aesthetic.
Amate and Nyaan wouldn't look out of place in a contemporary slice-of-life anime. This makes them relatable but also visually disconnected from the franchise's military sci-fi roots.
How GQuuuuuuX Connects to Other Gundam Series
While set in an alternate UC timeline, GQuuuuuuX constantly references the original Mobile Suit Gundam:
Char's role reversal:
Seeing Char as protagonist instead of antagonist reframes his motivations
Challia Bull's survival:
A character killed in episode 39 of the original series survives here, suggesting how small timeline changes cascade
Mobile suit redesigns:
The RX-78-2, Zaku, and other iconic mechas appear in Yamashita's reinterpreted forms
For Gundam veterans, these callbacks create a "familiar but wrong" feeling that enhances the alternate timeline's impact.
For newcomers, they're just cool mecha designs with no baggage attached.
The Music and Sound Design
Opening theme "Plazma" by Kenshi Yonezu became a hit in Japan, reaching high chart positions.
But reviews noted the soundtrack sometimes clashes with the show's tone—upbeat J-pop playing during tense combat feels incongruous, a tonal challenge that
even acclaimed anime sometimes struggle with
The voice acting cast includes:
Tomoyo Kurosawa
(Kumiko in Sound! Euphonium) as Amate
Yui Ishikawa
(Mikasa in Attack on Titan) as Nyaan
Shimba Tsuchiya
as Shuji
The English dub released simultaneously with Japanese audio on Prime Video—a first for Gundam series.
What Comes Next: Merchandise and Physical Releases
Gunpla Model Kits
Bandai has released multiple High Grade 1/144 model kits:
HG GQuuuuuuX
HG Red Gundam
(June 2025)
HG Police Zaku
(July 2025)
HG 01 Gundam [GQ]
HG Hambrabi (GQ)
(June 2026)
The GQuuuuuuX model features state-of-the-art articulation and flexibility showcased in promotional videos.
Home Video Releases
Three-volume releases launched in 2026:
Diskless editions
(¥8,800 each): Serial codes for digital extras, booklets, storyboards, no episodes
DVD editions
: 4 episodes per volume, booklets, non-credit OP/ED, Japanese and English subtitles
This marks the first "diskless" Gundam release, signaling industry shifts toward digital distribution.
Why 2026 Is GQuuuuuuX's Year
Though the series aired in 2025, its cultural impact extended into 2026:
Awards:
Won Japan Anime Trend Award and Animation of the Year at the 2026 Tokyo Anime Award Festival
Continued merchandising:
New Gunpla kits releasing throughout 2026
International expansion:
The series gained traction globally on Prime Video after its Japan-exclusive initial run
Convention presence:
Studio Khara announced a new short film at Japan Expo 2025, keeping momentum alive
The compressed 12-episode format actually helped its longevity—viewers can binge it in an afternoon, making it easier to recommend than 50-episode commitments.
The Verdict: A Bold Experiment That Mostly Works
Mobile Suit Gundam GQuuuuuuX won't replace your favorite Gundam series.
It's too short, too experimental, too deliberately divisive.
But it proves the franchise can evolve without abandoning what makes it Gundam—political complexity, war's human cost, and the symbolic power of giant robots.

The Evangelion creative team brought fresh energy to a 46-year-old franchise. Some experiments failed (tonal whiplash, rushed character development). Others succeeded (stunning animation, accessible alternate timeline, bold redesigns).
For newcomers intimidated by Gundam's vast continuity, GQuuuuuuX offers a 12-episode entry point that captures the franchise's themes without requiring homework.
For longtime fans, it's a fascinating "what if" that respects the original while fearlessly reimagining it—the kind of bold creative risk that made
Death Note still hit hard years after its release
That's rare in legacy franchises—and exactly why it became 2025's most viral anime.
Where to Watch:
Mobile Suit Gundam GQuuuuuuX is streaming exclusively on Prime Video with Japanese audio and English subtitles/dub.

children.text: Neon Genesis Evangelion (1995) disguises a deeply personal story about depression, loneliness, and identity crisis as a mecha anime. Creator Hideaki Anno channeled four years of clinical depression into the series, making protagonist Shinji Ikari's struggle to pilot the Eva a metaphor for living with mental illness. The giant robots aren't just war machines—they're literal prisons that trap pilots inside their own trauma. The series introduced the "Hedgehog's Dilemma" and "AT Fields" as frameworks for understanding why human connection feels impossible when you're depressed. Unlike typical mecha anime celebrating heroism, Evangelion asks: what if piloting the robot that saves humanity destroys the pilot's sense of self?
What Makes Evangelion Different From Other Mecha Anime

Neon Genesis Evangelion premiered in October 1995 as what appeared to be another giant robot anime. Humanity fights mysterious beings called Angels using biomechanical weapons called Evangelions, piloted by teenagers.
Then episode 4 aired.

The episode, titled "Hedgehog's Dilemma," featured almost no robot combat. Instead, it followed 14-year-old Shinji Ikari as he ran away from home, rode trains aimlessly, and sat alone in a movie theater—overwhelmed by anger he couldn't articulate. He listens to the same songs on repeat, going nowhere fast, pondering his place in life.
This wasn't how mecha anime worked. Where were the explosions? The strategic battles? The heroic speeches about protecting Earth?

What followed over 26 episodes wasn't a celebration of piloting giant robots. It was a psychological autopsy of what it costs to be the person everyone depends on when you can barely function yourself.
Hideaki Anno's Depression Became Shinji's Depression
The series exists because its creator spent four years unable to leave his house.

body.alt: How Neon Genesis Evangelion Uses Mecha to Explore Depression and Identity

children.text: Hideaki Anno suffered four years of clinical depression. In his own words: "I tried to include everything of myself in Neon Genesis Evangelion—myself, a broken man who could do nothing for four years. A man who ran away for four years, one who was simply not dead. Then one thought, 'You can't run away,' came to me, and I restarted this production."
Finding Words for What He Couldn't Name
Anno didn't initially understand he had depression. Mental health wasn't openly discussed in 1990s Japan—it was seen as weakness.

Halfway through production, creatively blocked while writing character Rei Ayanami, Anno asked a friend for reading suggestions about mental illness. The book he picked up startled him—it described his own problems. Anno had been struggling with depression for years without having the language for it.

This discovery transformed the series. What started as a standard mecha show became intensely autobiographical. Anno poured his self-loathing, isolation, and inability to connect directly into Shinji.

The result is a protagonist who feels nothing like typical anime heroes. Shinji doesn't want to save the world. He doesn't believe he can. He pilots the Eva because refusing feels worse than the terror of getting inside.
The Eva as Prison: When Your Body Becomes a Cage
In most mecha anime, piloting a giant robot represents power and agency. In Evangelion, it's the opposite.
The Evangelion units are biomechanical—part machine, part living organism. Pilots don't control them so much as synchronize their nervous systems with them, experiencing the Eva's pain as their own.
Trapped Inside the Thing That's Supposed to Save You

Shinji is a helpless boy trapped inside a killing machine. This captures depression's specific horror—you're trapped inside a body that's supposed to keep you alive but instead makes living feel impossible.
The Eva becomes a visual metaphor for dissociation: being present but disconnected, going through motions while feeling absent from your own life.

In episode 18, Unit-01 goes berserk and eats an Angel while Shinji screams inside the entry plug, unable to stop his own body from committing violence. He's a passenger in something that wears his shape but doesn't respond to his will.
Similar to
Welcome to the NHK's portrayal of social anxiety as paralysis
, Evangelion shows how mental illness doesn't just affect your thoughts—it hijacks your entire physical existence.
The Hedgehog's Dilemma: Why Connection Feels Impossible
Episode 4 introduces a concept that becomes the series' emotional foundation: the Hedgehog's Dilemma.

Dr. Ritsuko Akagi explains it: "Hedgehogs have a hard time sharing warmth with other hedgehogs. The closer they get, the more they hurt each other with their quills. People are also like that. Some part of Shinji is afraid to take that risk because he's afraid of being hurt."
The Depression Paradox

This perfectly describes depression's cruel logic: you desperately need connection but believe you'll contaminate anyone who gets close. Every attempt at intimacy feels like a threat—to yourself and others.

Shinji pushes away every person who tries to care about him, not because he doesn't want their warmth but because he's convinced proximity to him will hurt them. His quills aren't defensive mechanisms he consciously deploys. They're intrinsic to his sense of self.
AT Fields: The Literal Barriers Around Our Identities
The series' most brilliant metaphorical device is the AT Field—Absolute Terror Field.
In-universe, AT Fields are force fields that protect both Angels and Evangelions during combat. But the name reveals their real function.
The term A.T. Field stands for 'Absolute Terror Field.' What does it mean for an entire person to be held together by terror?
What Holds You Together Also Keeps You Alone

The AT Field represents psychological boundaries—the walls we build around our identities to protect ourselves from being known, judged, or abandoned. They symbolize barriers that separate one individual from another, keeping their thoughts private.

When you're depressed, these boundaries become prison walls. Your AT Field protects you from vulnerability but also ensures you remain isolated. You can't let anyone in without risking annihilation of the fragile self you've constructed.
This connects to
how Mushishi shows that some problems aren't meant to be fixed
—sometimes the thing keeping you alive is also the thing keeping you alone.
Every Character Suffers Different Symptoms of the Same Disease
Shinji isn't the only one trapped by depression and trauma. Every major character demonstrates a different manifestation of mental illness:
Rei Ayanami: Dissociation and Questioning Existence

Rei exhibits symptoms of dissociation and depersonalization. She doesn't value her own life because she doesn't believe she has a real self to value. Her question "Am I real?" isn't philosophical—it's the desperate plea of someone who can't feel their own existence.
Asuka Langley Soryu: Compensatory Ego and Fear of Worthlessness

Asuka is Shinji's opposite—aggressively confident, competitive, desperate to prove her value through performance. But her bravado is armor protecting the same wound Shinji bears openly: the belief that she's fundamentally unlovable.

When her sync rate drops and she can no longer pilot effectively, her entire identity collapses. She attempts suicide. The thing she used to prove her worth becomes impossible, leaving nothing underneath.
This mirrors
the crushing pressure in Hajime no Ippo when your entire identity becomes what you achieve
Misato Katsuragi: Functional Depression and Avoidance

Misato functions in society. She has a job, maintains relationships, appears normal. But she drinks heavily, avoids emotional intimacy, and uses sexual attention as validation rather than connection. Her functionality doesn't mean she's healed. It means she's better at hiding.
The Human Instrumentality Project: When Isolation Becomes Unbearable
The series' final act introduces the Human Instrumentality Project—a plan to merge all human consciousness into a single unified being to banish loneliness forever.
The Fantasy of No Longer Being Separate
SEELE created the Project to unite humanity into one consciousness. Wars and conflict would be erased, but at the cost of individuality.

For someone suffering profound loneliness and self-loathing, the promise of dissolving your separate self into an ocean of shared consciousness where you can never be rejected or abandoned sounds like relief.
Instrumentality isn't presented as villainy. It's presented as euthanasia for identity—a permanent solution to the pain of being a separate, vulnerable self.
Episodes 25 & 26: The Therapy Session Ending

The original series' final two episodes abandoned external plot entirely. Instead, they take place almost entirely inside Shinji's mind as he undergoes something resembling group therapy during Instrumentality.
Deconstructing Identity Under Depression
The episodes ask Shinji to examine his core beliefs: "I'm worthless," "Nobody wants me here," "I only exist to be used by others."

The episodes systematically challenge these beliefs, showing that Shinji's depression distorts reality. No one ever told Shinji he's not lovable, no one told him that he is a failure. His father didn't summon him to hurt him—Gendo is simply incapable of expressing care.
The "Congratulations" Scene
The series ends with Shinji accepting that he wants to exist as himself, flaws and all. Everyone applauds. "Congratulations!"

For viewers expecting narrative closure, this felt like a betrayal. For viewers recognizing depression, it felt painfully honest. Recovery isn't defeating your demons. It's deciding to live despite them.
The End of Evangelion: The Relapse
Fans reacted poorly to the original ending. Some sent death threats.

Anno's response was The End of Evangelion (1997)—a film showing what "actually" happened during those final episodes. It's cynical and deeply depressing, showing the darkest possible version of events.
The Darkest Possible Version
The film is brutal. Shinji sexually assaults comatose Asuka. The military massacres Nerv personnel. Giant Rei's decapitated head floats through space bleeding across the stars.
Shinji still rejects Instrumentality. He still chooses individual existence over eternal unity.
But the film's final image is Shinji strangling Asuka on a beach littered with corpses before she reaches up to caress his face. He collapses. She says: "Disgusting."
Recovery Isn't Linear

Shinji still comes to the same conclusion—that he wants to live and be with others, in spite of the suffering it may cause. But it's clear he still has a long way to go in fixing his broken mental state.

The End of Evangelion acknowledges that having a breakthrough doesn't fix everything. Shinji's decision to live doesn't erase his capacity for harm, his self-loathing, or his broken relationships. It just means he's choosing to exist in that brokenness rather than escape it.
This brutal honesty is why the film endures—similar to
how Chainsaw Man feels empty and wrong on purpose
Why Evangelion's Approach to Mental Health Matters
Mental health is brought up frequently these days, but in 1997, it was a taboo subject. This is part of why Neon Genesis Evangelion is so vital in the conversation about mental health.
Before Evangelion, anime heroes struggled with tactical problems—defeating enemies, protecting friends, saving worlds. Internal struggles were obstacles to overcome on the way to victory.
Evangelion made internal struggle the entire point.
The Series Doesn't Offer Solutions

What makes Evangelion valuable isn't that it teaches you how to fix depression. It's that it shows depression accurately—the self-loathing that feels like truth, the isolation that seems like protection, the fantasy of disappearing completely.

For many viewers, especially those who watched it as teenagers, Evangelion was the first time they saw their internal experience reflected in fiction. One viewer wrote after watching Shinji's silent train ride in episode 4: "A TV show helped me understand something about my own mental health for the first time."
Recognition Isn't Recovery, But It's a Start

The series doesn't promise healing. Shinji ends both the TV series and End of Evangelion still damaged, still struggling, still capable of hurting himself and others. But he's chosen to keep existing.

That's not inspirational in the traditional sense. It's just honest. And for people living with depression, that honesty can be more valuable than false hope—recognition that the struggle doesn't end, you just find ways to live alongside it.
This connects to
why Reigen Arataka works as one of anime's best-written adults
—flawed people trying to function despite not having everything figured out.
The Giant Robots Were Never the Point

Neon Genesis Evangelion uses its mecha framework as elaborate metaphor. The Angels represent existential threats. The Evas represent bodies you're forced to inhabit. The AT Fields represent the terror that holds your identity intact.
But strip away the sci-fi imagery and you have a story about a depressed teenager who can't connect with others, doesn't value his own life, and has to choose whether existence is worth its pain.

The genius is hiding that story inside a genre typically defined by power fantasies and heroic triumph. Anno weaponized audience expectations. You came for giant robots saving humanity. You got a dissection of what it costs to save yourself when you don't believe you're worth saving.

Nearly three decades later, Evangelion remains essential viewing not despite its refusal to provide answers, but because of it. It trusts viewers to sit with discomfort, to recognize themselves in Shinji's struggle, and to understand that choosing to exist—however imperfectly—is its own kind of heroism.
No giant robot required.
Where to Watch:
Neon Genesis Evangelion and The End of Evangelion are streaming on Netflix with English subtitles and dub.

children.text: Bakugo and Deku's rivalry in My Hero Academia isn't about who's stronger—it's about who they are when strength stops defining them. Bakugo's entire identity was built on being superior to everyone, especially Quirkless Deku. When Deku gains One For All and starts surpassing him, Bakugo doesn't just face defeat in competition—he faces the collapse of his entire sense of self. The rivalry explores what happens when your worth is tied to being the best, when the person you looked down on becomes your equal, and when you're forced to rebuild who you are from scratch. Unlike typical shonen rivalries driven by power scaling, Bakugo and Deku's relationship asks: if you're not the strongest, who are you?
Bakugo didn’t lose to Deku. He lost the story he told himself about who he was.
Streaming on Crunchyroll and Funimation.
The Rivalry That Doesn't Follow the Rules

Most shonen rivalries follow a template: two powerful characters push each other to greater heights through competition. Goku and Vegeta. Naruto and Sasuke. The formula works because both rivals start roughly equal.
Bakugo and Deku break this completely.
Their rivalry begins when one has everything and the other has nothing—built on the assumption that gap will never close.
The Childhood That Set Everything
Bakugo gained an inflated ego from being praised excessively for his powerful Explosion Quirk, leading him to bully Quirkless Izuku Midoriya.
But the bullying wasn't just cruelty. It was self-defense.
When they were children, Deku tried to help Bakugo after he fell into a river. Bakugo was offended that a weakling like Deku tried to save him and assumed he was looking down on him.
This moment reveals everything. Bakugo's entire identity rested on being superior. A Quirkless kid offering help shattered that hierarchy—so Bakugo rebuilt the wall with violence and contempt.
The nickname "Deku" (meaning useless) wasn't just an insult. It was Bakugo's attempt to permanently define someone who threatened his sense of self.
When Your Identity Is Built on Being Better
Katsuki started out believing his worth was tied to how strong he was.

In My Hero Academia's society, Quirks determine value. Heroes are celebrities. Power equals worth. Bakugo absorbed this completely—his Explosion Quirk made him special, and being special became his entire personality.
The Problem With Conditional Self-Worth
When your identity depends on external validation—being the strongest, smartest, most talented—you're building on sand. Any threat to that superiority threatens your entire existence.
Deku represented the ultimate threat: proof that Bakugo's superiority wasn't inherent. If a Quirkless nobody could become his equal, then Bakugo was never special—he just got lucky with genetics.
This connects to
how comparing yourself to others destroys you in The Pet Girl of Sakurasou
—when your worth depends on being better than someone else, you're always one comparison away from collapse.
The Identity Crisis Disguised as Competition
In Episode 8, Deku defeated Bakugo in a practice exercise. But Bakugo lost not because of his power but because of his arrogance and inability to work as a team.
This wasn't just a loss in training. It was existential annihilation.

Bakugo's entire worldview rested on a hierarchy where he stood at the top and Deku at the bottom. When Deku wins—not through luck but through qualities Bakugo dismissed as weakness (teamwork, strategy, empathy)—the entire structure collapses.
What Bakugo Actually Lost

body.alt: Bakugo's Rivalry with Deku Is About Identity

children.text: He didn't lose a fight. He lost the story he'd been telling himself about who he was.
After he loses to Deku, feels he can't measure up to Todoroki, gets kidnapped, and fails his Licensing Exam, he suffers a massive identity crisis that knocks down his fragile confidence.
Each defeat chips away at the foundation. If strength doesn't guarantee victory, what does it guarantee? If being talented doesn't make you special, what does?
Similar to
how Haikyuu explores effort without a promise of greatness
, Bakugo discovers that natural talent without growth is a dead end.
Why Bakugo Can't Just "Get Stronger"
In a typical shonen rivalry, the solution to falling behind is training harder. Get a new technique. Unlock a transformation. Close the gap through effort.
Bakugo does train harder. He does get stronger. It doesn't fix anything.
The Problem Isn't Power—It's Perspective

If he isn't the strongest and he isn't meant to achieve immediate greatness, then what is his role? It's something that Quirkless Midoriya had to evaluate for many years as a child. What is his purpose in a world that seems destined to leave him behind?
Bakugo is forced to ask the same question Deku asked his entire childhood: who am I if I'm not what I thought I was?
For Deku, that question led to discovering identity beyond Quirks—heroism as action, not status. For Bakugo, it requires dismantling everything he built his personality on.
What Deku Has That Bakugo Doesn't
The series explicitly contrasts their approaches to All Might, their shared idol.
While Deku admired All Might's ability to save lives with a smile, Bakugo admired his strength and ability to defeat anyone.
This difference is everything.
Two Different Definitions of Heroism
Deku sees heroism as connection—reaching people, protecting them, making them feel safe.
Bakugo sees heroism as dominance—being strong enough that threats don't matter, proving yourself through victory.
Neither is wrong, but only one is complete.
Endeavor has a powerful quirk and is skilled at rescuing civilians, but the reason why he's unable to surpass All Might is because he fundamentally does not care about the people he's saving.
Bakugo mirrors Endeavor—technically excellent, strategically brilliant, but missing the emotional core that makes All Might irreplaceable.
The rivalry with Deku forces Bakugo to develop what he lacks: empathy, collaboration, the ability to see strength in vulnerability.
The Fight That Changes Everything
Their second major fight—where Bakugo finally admits his feelings—is when the rivalry transforms completely.
Bakugo breaks down. He admits he feels responsible for All Might's retirement. He admits he doesn't understand how Deku got his Quirk. He admits he feels left behind.
Vulnerability as Strength
For someone whose entire identity was built on never showing weakness, this moment is death and rebirth.

Bakugo's ceaseless drive forces Midoriya to become more assertive, and he eventually welcomes the rivalry. Meanwhile, Midoriya's attitude forces Bakugo into a previously unforeseen habit of contemplation.
They're not just making each other stronger. They're making each other more complete.
Deku learns confidence and assertiveness from Bakugo's refusal to back down. Bakugo learns empathy and teamwork from Deku's instinctive heroism.
This parallels
how Kids on the Slope shows that relationships force us to grow in unexpected ways
—growth doesn't require perfection, just willingness to change.
The Ending: Choosing to Redefine Yourself
By the series' conclusion, Bakugo's transformation is complete—not because he's the strongest, but because he's rebuilt his identity on different foundations.

Bakugo has been a proponent in crafting technology that allows Midoriya to potentially take a physically active role in superheroism again, meaning that the boy who once insulted a character without "powers" has now evolved into a man who wishes to find a way to bring those abilities back.
From Contempt to Support
The Bakugo who bullied Quirkless Deku now dedicates himself to helping Quirkless Deku become a hero again. Not because he pities him. Because he respects him.
His identity is no longer built on being superior to Deku. It's built on being Deku's equal—someone who pushes him forward not through competition but through collaboration.
The rivalry doesn't end. It evolves into partnership.
Similar to
how Bakuman shows the hidden costs of creative ambition
, Bakugo discovers that identity built on relationships is stronger than identity built on dominance.
What the Rivalry Actually Teaches
Bakugo and Deku's relationship isn't about friendship conquering all or rivals becoming brothers.
It's about what happens when the person you built your entire identity around surpasses you—and you're forced to decide who you are without that hierarchy.
The Uncomfortable Truth About Conditional Identity

Most people build identity on external markers: job titles, achievements, being better than peers. When those markers shift—when you get fired, when someone younger surpasses you, when your talent stops being enough—you face the same crisis Bakugo does.
Who are you when the thing that made you special becomes common? When your worth can't be measured by comparison?
The series doesn't offer easy answers. Bakugo's growth takes the entire series. He relapses into old patterns. He struggles with anger management.
But he rebuilds anyway—slowly, imperfectly, honestly.
This connects to
why Eren started the Rumbling beyond just protecting Paradis
—real growth is messy, incomplete, and driven by complex motivations beyond simple heroism.
The Rivalry That Saved Both of Them

Both young heroes look at the world's number 1 hero for inspiration. While their end goals were the same, the two determined they needed different things to get to their goals. However, as the story progresses both begin to realize that they each lack what the other has.
Deku needed Bakugo's confidence, his refusal to accept limits, his aggressive drive to win. Bakugo needed Deku's empathy, his collaborative spirit, his instinct to save rather than defeat.
Neither could become a complete hero alone. The rivalry forced them both to develop what they lacked—not through competition, but through recognition.
By the end, they're not trying to surpass each other. They're trying to become worthy of standing beside each other.
That's not a rivalry about competition. That's a rivalry about identity—and it's exactly why it works.

children.text: Anime fights aren't just action — at their best, they're the moment every emotional thread in a story pulls taut. The greatest ones hit you somewhere deep: about identity, sacrifice, obsession, grief. This list isn't ranked by choreography alone. It's ranked by how hard each fight
meant something
If you want to see where these shows rank overall, check out our breakdown of the
Top 10 Most Popular Anime of All Time, Ranked by Fans in 2026
1. Gojo Satoru vs Ryomen Sukuna — Jujutsu Kaisen

Studio MAPPA delivered something that redefined what TV animation could look like. The clash between the strongest sorcerer and the king of curses wasn't just visually overwhelming — it was two philosophies of power colliding at full force. Every domain expansion, every reversal, every quiet second before a technique felt earned. It broke streaming records and shattered the fandom in ways nobody saw coming.
The outcome of this fight still ripples through the entire JJK story. If you want to understand what came after, read our deep dive on
whether Megumi Fushiguro is actually dead in JJK
2. Rengoku vs Akaza — Demon Slayer: Mugen Train

Ufotable turned in one of the most visually spectacular sequences in anime history, but what makes Rengoku vs Akaza immortal is emotional weight. A Flame Hashira who burns bright refusing to be extinguished — even against an Upper Moon who hasn't lost in centuries. The sunrise. The final breath. The words he leaves behind. Audiences wept in cinemas worldwide.

body.alt: Best Anime Fights of All Time - Naruto vs Sasuke Final Valley Battle

children.text: Demon Slayer's animation has always been its strongest card. We compared it head-to-head in
JJK vs Demon Slayer: Animation, Story, and Power System Compared
. And if you're excited about what's coming next, here's why
the Infinity Castle arc could break every anime record
3. Naruto vs Pain — Naruto Shippuden

The Pain Invasion Arc is Naruto's darkest chapter, and its climax delivered completely. Naruto's Nine-Tails release, the moment he nearly crosses a line he can't return from, and then the conversation that follows the fight — this is storytelling that uses action to reach something deeper about pain, belief, and cycles of hatred. Older fans still call it Naruto's single greatest moment.
We wrote a full breakdown of why
the Pain Invasion Arc was Naruto at its absolute darkest
. And if you want to go further into the Naruto lore rabbit hole, our piece on
why Sasuke betrayed Konoha
is essential reading.
4. Gon vs Neferpitou — Hunter × Hunter

This isn't a fight in the traditional sense. It's a breakdown. Gon transforming into something unrecognizable — burning his future, his potential, his life — just to reach a power capable of destruction on that scale. It's one of anime's most disturbing moments precisely because the protagonist isn't heroic here. He's terrifying. Yoshihiro Togashi wrote Gon doing something no shonen hero is supposed to do.
Neferpitou's arc connects directly to one of HxH's most morally complex characters. Our essay on
why Meruem is more human than the hunters
explores the same thematic thread.
5. Ichigo vs Ulquiorra — Bleach (Hollow Form)
The rooftop fight in Hueco Mundo remains one of the most visually haunting in Bleach's run. Ichigo losing, dying, and then
something else

taking over — a hollow so powerful it terrifies even Ulquiorra. The atmosphere is completely different from any fight before it. Dark, desperate, and genuinely scary. Ulquiorra asking what a heart is, in his final moments, still hits years later.
Bleach has been on one of anime's greatest comeback runs. Here's our full piece on
why Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War is the perfect anime comeback
, and a look at
why Yhwach is the most dangerous villain Bleach ever created
6. Sasuke vs Itachi — Naruto Shippuden

Years of buildup, years of hatred, and then the truth. The Sasuke vs Itachi fight works on two levels at once — as a technically stunning ninja battle and as the moment an entire character's worldview collapses. Itachi's final gesture is one of anime's most heartbreaking images. Even rewatching it knowing everything, it stings.
For more on how Sasuke's arc continues to divide fans, read our breakdown of
the real story behind Sasuke's betrayal of Konoha
. We also looked at the eternal debate:
Itachi vs Jiraiya — who was actually stronger?
7. Levi vs the Beast Titan — Attack on Titan Season 3

Three minutes of animation. That's roughly how long Levi's assault on the Beast Titan lasts. It is, by most measures, the most technically perfect action sequence in the entire series — fluid, brutal, and edited with the precision of a horror film. Zeke doesn't even process what happens to him. Neither does the audience, the first time through.
Attack on Titan remains culturally massive even years after its ending. We explored exactly
why AoT is still popular in 2026
, and unpacked
why Eren started the Rumbling — and why it wasn't just for Paradis
8. Spike vs Vincent — Cowboy Bebop: Knockin' on Heaven's Door

Often overlooked in these lists because it's from the film rather than the series, but the Spike vs Vincent fight in the movie is everything Cowboy Bebop promised from the beginning. Cold, stylish, and steeped in a shared sense of exhaustion. Two men who shouldn't still be alive, fighting like they've already accepted what's coming. The jazz score does half the work.
9. Mugen, Jin, and Fuu vs the Shogunate Assassins — Samurai Champloo (Final Arc)

The three-fight finale of Samurai Champloo gives each character their own closing statement. Mugen's is chaos. Jin's is precision. Both are beautiful. Shinichiro Watanabe understands that how someone fights is a complete expression of who they are — and the ending sequences prove it completely.
If swordsmanship in anime interests you, we also ranked the
strongest anime swordsmen of all time in the 2026 edition
10. Rock Lee vs Gaara — Naruto (Chunin Exams)

No powers. No bloodline ability. Just a boy who was told he'd never be a real ninja, taking off ankle weights and showing the world what pure effort looks like. Rock Lee vs Gaara is still the best argument anime has ever made for training, determination, and the emotional stakes of someone with nothing to fall back on except work. It holds up completely after 20+ years.
Honorable Mentions
These didn't make the top 10 but deserve every bit of recognition:
Thorfinn vs Askeladd
(Vinland Saga) — grief dressed as combat. If you haven't seen Vinland Saga yet, check out
the best anime to watch if you loved it
Mob's 100% Explosion
(Mob Psycho 100) — Reigen's role in this moment is why we wrote about
why Reigen is one of anime's best written adults
Bakugo vs Deku
(My Hero Academia) — more than a fight, it's a therapy session. Read our piece on
why Bakugo's rivalry with Deku is about identity, not competition
Sung Jin-Woo vs Thomas Andre
(Solo Leveling) — for more on where Solo Leveling stands overall, we wrote about
why it feels overhyped after the first arc
Final Thoughts

The best anime fights aren't the most explosive ones. They're the ones that make you feel something you didn't expect — dread, grief, awe, or the strange ache of watching someone burn everything just to reach an impossible moment. Every fight on this list does exactly that.

children.text: Hay peleas que simplemente se ven bien y luego están las que se te clavan en el alma. Las que van más allá de la animación espectacular y te golpean con emociones, ideologías enfrentadas y decisiones irreversibles. Esta lista no se centra en quién gana, sino en las peleas que se sienten más intensas, más profundas y más memorables.
1. Gojo Satoru vs Sukuna — Jujutsu Kaisen

La pelea que rompió internet y elevó el estándar del anime moderno. Más allá de la brutal animación de MAPPA, destaca la tensión constante y el peligro real. Gojo, el hombre que parecía invencible, se enfrenta por fin a alguien a su nivel.
Relacionado:
¿Está muerto Megumi Fushiguro en Jujutsu Kaisen?
2. Rengoku Kyojuro vs Akaza — Demon Slayer

No importa quién gane, importa la dignidad con la que se mantiene firme. Rengoku pelea sabiendo su destino y lo hace brillar como pocos. El amanecer y sus últimas palabras convierten esta batalla en una de las despedidas más emotivas del anime.

body.alt: Top 10 Mejores Peleas de Anime de Todos los Tiempos (2026)

children.text: Relacionado:
Jujutsu Kaisen vs Demon Slayer: Animación, historia y sistemas de poder comparados
y
Demon Slayer: Infinity Castle, ¿por qué el arco final podría romper todos los récords?
3. Naruto vs Pain — Naruto Shippuden

El punto de madurez real de Naruto. No es solo la acción, es el brutal enfrentamiento de ideales y el diálogo posterior que redefine al personaje. Pain Invasion sigue siendo uno de los arcos más oscuros y profundos de la serie.
Relacionado:
El arco de la invasión de Pain fue Naruto en su momento más oscuro
4. Gon vs Neferpitou — Hunter x Hunter
Esto no es una pelea, es una tragedia. Gon sacrifica su humanidad y su futuro por venganza. Cruda, incómoda y dolorosa, es una de las rupturas de personaje mejor escritas en el anime.
Relacionado:
¿Por qué Meruem es más humano que los cazadores?
5. Ichigo vs Ulquiorra — Bleach
Oscura, salvaje y psicológica. El Hollow completo de Ichigo transforma al héroe en algo aterrador. Ulquiorra, que nunca entendió las emociones humanas, termina cuestionando su propia existencia.
Relacionado:
¿Por qué Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War es el regreso perfecto del anime?
y
Yhwach es el villano más peligroso que ha creado Bleach
6. Sasuke vs Itachi — Naruto Shippuden
Años de odio, mentiras y sufrimiento explotan en un duelo legendario. La pelea es excelente, pero el verdadero impacto llega con la revelación final que destroza todo lo que Sasuke creía.
Relacionado:
¿Por qué Sasuke traicionó a Konoha? La verdadera historia explicada
y
Itachi vs Jiraiya: ¿Quién era realmente más fuerte?
7. Levi Ackerman vs Titán Bestia — Attack on Titan
Corta, precisa y devastadora. Levi en estado puro: ejecución quirúrgica sin discursos innecesarios. Una de las secuencias más satisfactorias y brutales de todo el anime.
Relacionado:
¿Por qué Attack on Titan sigue siendo tan popular en 2026?
8. Spike Spiegel vs Vincent Volaju — Cowboy Bebop
Fría, melancólica y existencial. Dos hombres rotos que ya no tienen nada que perder. Los golpes pesan más por el vacío emocional que transmiten.
9. Mugen vs Jin — Samurai Champloo
Caos descontrolado contra precisión letal. Dos filosofías de vida completamente opuestas chocando en un cierre de serie elegante y perfecto.
10. Rock Lee vs Gaara — Naruto
La pelea más inspiradora de la historia del anime. Un ninja sin talento innato que lo da absolutamente todo con esfuerzo puro. Demuestra que la voluntad puede hacer temblar hasta a los monstruos.
Relacionado:
Los espadachines más fuertes del anime de todos los tiempos (Edición 2026)
Menciones Honoríficas
Thorfinn vs Askeladd (Vinland Saga) → Más dolor y odio que combate.
Mob al 100% (Mob Psycho 100) → Explosión emocional pura.
Deku vs Bakugo (My Hero Academia) → Más reconciliación que pelea.
Sung Jin-Woo vs Thomas Andre (Solo Leveling) → Poder abrumador.
Relacionado:
¿Puede Sung Jin-Woo vencer a Goku?
Conclusión

Las mejores peleas de anime no siempre son las más largas o espectaculares. Son aquellas que te hacen sentir rabia, tristeza, inspiración o vacío. Las que dejan de ser solo acción y se convierten en momentos inolvidables de la historia.

children.text: The Seven Great Powers are the most famous combat ranking in
Mushoku Tensei: Jobless Reincarnation
: seven legendary positions associated with warriors whose strength sits far beyond ordinary adventurers, mages, and swordsmen. At the point when the ranking is introduced, the order is
Technique God, Dragon God, Fighting God, Demon God, Death God, Sword God, and North God

That list looks simple. The lore behind it is not. A position can change hands, a title is not necessarily the same thing as a conventional magic or swordsmanship rank, and the number beside a name should not be treated as a perfect mathematical measurement of every possible matchup.

This guide explains the Seven Great Powers in their established order, what makes each position frightening, and why Orsted complicates any attempt to read the monuments as an infallible strongest-character list.
Major Light Novel Spoiler Warning:

The sections below discuss identities, abilities, and developments well beyond the currently adapted anime material. Anime-only viewers should stop after the quick table if they want to avoid future-story spoilers.
Quick Ranking: Who Are the Seven Great Powers?

| Rank | Title | Holder at the ranking’s introduction | Defining threat | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Technique God | Technique God Laplace | Extraordinary combat knowledge and technique | | 2 | Dragon God | Orsted | Overwhelming all-round combat ability | | 3 | Fighting God | Fighting God / Fighting God Armor | Extreme physical combat and armor-based power | | 4 | Demon God | Demon God Laplace | Enormous magical power and destructive potential | | 5 | Death God | Randolph Marianne | Lethal, deceptive swordsmanship | | 6 | Sword God | Gal Farion | Supreme offensive sword speed and technique | | 7 | North God | Aleksander Rybak, Kalman III | Adaptability, unusual techniques, and battlefield versatility |

The first detail worth noticing is Laplace. The Technique God and Demon God are connected to the two halves produced by the division of the original Demon Dragon God Laplace. That is why “Laplace” can appear twice in discussions of the Seven Great Powers without the ranking simply duplicating one person.
How the Seven Great Powers Ranking Works

The Seven Great Powers were established after the Second Human-Demon War. Technique God created the ranking and monuments bearing the emblems of the seven powers serve as the world’s record of those positions. When the holder of a position changes through the system’s rules, the monuments update accordingly.

body.alt: Mushoku Tensei - Monument of the Seven Great World Powers

children.text: This makes the list more than folklore. In-universe, it is an institution with history and succession.
But it has an important limitation:
rank is not a complete combat equation
Mushoku Tensei

repeatedly treats strength as a combination of technique, equipment, information, matchup, preparation, experience, and circumstance. The Seven Great Powers identify exceptional fighters, but a lower number does not automatically answer every hypothetical duel.
That distinction matters most near the top of the list.
1. Technique God — Laplace
Technique God occupies the first position on the Seven Great Powers monuments. This identity is associated with the technique-oriented half of Laplace after the Demon Dragon God was split.

The title is fitting. Where the Demon God side is associated with tremendous magical capacity, Technique God represents the accumulated martial knowledge and technical side of Laplace. The threat is therefore not merely raw destructive output. It is mastery: knowledge of fighting methods and the ability to understand combat at a level almost nobody else can approach.
Why Technique God Is Ranked First
Technique God’s placement reflects the historical ranking created after the great war. As the figure who established the Seven Great Powers, Technique God sits at the summit of the monument system.
That does
not
mean readers should automatically conclude that Technique God defeats Orsted under every set of conditions. The ranking is a canonical hierarchy, but
Mushoku Tensei
gives enough context around Orsted to make “rank one equals guaranteed winner” too simplistic.
Core advantage:
unparalleled technical knowledge.
Main uncertainty:
much of Technique God’s practical combat ceiling is deliberately less visible than that of characters who fight extensively in the main story.
2. Dragon God — Orsted
Orsted is the character who most clearly demonstrates why the Seven Great Powers should not be read like numerical RPG stats.

As Dragon God, he combines extraordinary physical ability, Dragon Tribe techniques, magic, swordsmanship, battle knowledge, and terrifying efficiency. His encounters establish a huge gap between elite fighters and the level occupied by the very strongest beings in the setting.

Orsted is especially dangerous because he is not dependent on one trick. Against a swordsman, he has the speed and technique to engage directly. Against magic, he possesses knowledge and counters. Against unfamiliar situations, his experience gives him an informational advantage that most opponents simply cannot reproduce.
Is Orsted Actually Stronger Than the No. 1 Technique God?
This is where a careful ranking needs to separate
official position
from
editorial combat assessment

Officially, Orsted is No. 2. In practical discussions of the strongest active combatants, however, he has a compelling claim to be the most dangerous fighter readers actually see operating in the main story. His limits are also tied to circumstances larger than a single duel, meaning he does not always fight as though spending every resource is irrelevant.
So the cleanest conclusion is:
Technique God is canonically ranked first, while Orsted can reasonably be treated as the benchmark for demonstrated all-round combat supremacy.
Those statements are not contradictory.
Core advantage:
the best overall combination of power, technique, knowledge, and versatility.
Main limitation:
resource management matters to Orsted in ways that a simple one-off versus debate often ignores.
3. Fighting God — The Fighting God Armor
The third position is unusual because the Fighting God’s terrifying reputation is inseparable from the
Fighting God Armor

. The armor is not just defensive equipment. It is a combat system capable of turning its wearer into a relentless physical threat, and later light-novel material makes its importance impossible to ignore.

Badigadi is closely associated with the Fighting God role in the story, but it is more precise to understand the rank through the armor and the state produced when it is fully brought into battle rather than treating “Badigadi without context” as automatically equivalent to the No. 3 position.
Why the Fighting God Is So Difficult to Beat

The key problem is persistence. Tremendous strength is only part of the equation. A fighter facing the Fighting God must deal with the armor’s capabilities, the wearer’s durability and endurance, and the difficulty of ending the battle cleanly.

That makes this rank a good example of matchup-based power. A character may possess devastating attacks and still lack the specific combination of knowledge, damage, and staying power needed to secure a decisive victory.
Core advantage:
overwhelming armor-assisted physical combat and endurance.
Main limitation:
the exact threat depends heavily on the wearer and the armor’s state.
4. Demon God — Laplace
Demon God Laplace is the magic-oriented half of the divided Demon Dragon God Laplace and one of the central historical threats hanging over the world of
Mushoku Tensei

If Technique God represents knowledge and martial technique, Demon God represents the other terrifying inheritance: immense magical power. His place at No. 4 should not make him seem remotely ordinary compared with the top three. The upper end of the Seven Great Powers operates on a scale where differences in history, condition, and matchup matter as much as a neat numbered ladder.

Demon God Laplace also matters beyond power scaling. His existence shapes nations, racial tensions, military planning, and the long-term direction of the story. Few names in the setting carry comparable historical weight.
Core advantage:
colossal magical capability and mana.
Main limitation:
the divided Laplace does not possess the complete set of qualities associated with the original Demon Dragon God.
5. Death God — Randolph Marianne

Randolph Marianne is where the ranking begins to feel more recognizably human in scale, but “more human” should not be confused with weak. As Death God, Randolph is a veteran whose danger comes from lethal swordsmanship, experience, deception, and the ability to make opponents hesitate or misread what is happening.
That psychological component is important.
Mushoku Tensei
does not reserve strength for the person who can create the largest explosion. A fighter who controls the opponent’s decisions can manufacture an opening before the decisive attack even begins.
Why Randolph Is More Dangerous Than His Rank Suggests

Randolph’s style punishes straightforward power comparisons. Against an opponent who knows exactly what he does, some of his advantages can be reduced. Against someone encountering his methods without preparation, his tricks and presence become much more dangerous.
This is precisely why ranking characters only by destructive output misses how combat works in this series.
Core advantage:
experience, lethal technique, and psychological disruption.
Main limitation:
information about his methods can reduce the surprise that makes them especially effective.
6. Sword God — Gal Farion
Gal Farion represents the brutal philosophy of the Sword God Style: seize the initiative and end the fight before the opponent can establish their own game plan.

At its highest level, the style’s famous offensive techniques turn speed and commitment into killing power. Gal is therefore one of the clearest examples of a specialist among the Seven Great Powers. He does not need the broad magical toolkit associated with Orsted or Laplace if his first decisive exchange ends the battle.
Why the Sword God Can Threaten Higher-Ranked Opponents
Initiative matters. A ranking can say one fighter is stronger overall, but that does not make them immune to a swordsman whose entire discipline is built around an overwhelmingly fast opening attack.
Gal’s weakness is the reverse side of that specialization. If an opponent survives, reads, counters, or prevents the ideal offensive exchange, the matchup becomes much less comfortable.
Core advantage:
extraordinary offensive speed and one-strike lethality.
Main limitation:
a highly aggressive style creates matchup dependencies against opponents who can neutralize the opening attack.
7. North God — Aleksander Rybak, Kalman III
Aleksander Rybak, commonly identified as
North God Kalman III

, holds the seventh position when the Seven Great Powers are introduced. His placement at No. 7 is one of the best warnings against interpreting “seventh” as merely the weakest member of a static list.

The North God Style prizes adaptability. Its practitioners are associated with unconventional weapons, tricks, situational tactics, and a willingness to win without insisting on a clean textbook duel. At the highest level, that flexibility makes a North God difficult to prepare for.
Later material also gives Aleksander circumstances and equipment that can dramatically alter how dangerous he is. In other words, the version of a character being compared matters.
Core advantage:
adaptability, unusual techniques, and versatility.
Main limitation:
his effectiveness varies significantly with experience, equipment, and the exact stage of the story.
Are the Seven Great Powers Literally the Seven Strongest Characters?
Not in the simplistic sense that the list permanently contains the seven beings who would win every possible one-on-one fight.

The monuments represent a recognized ranking system with succession rules and history. They do not continuously simulate every character’s current condition, hidden ability, equipment, matchup, or tactical circumstances. Nor does a title automatically tell us how a battle unfolds when one fighter has advance knowledge of another.
A better way to read the Seven Great Powers is as
Mushoku Tensei’s legendary combat hierarchy
. Reaching it means entering the setting’s highest recognized class of warriors. Within that class, however, context still matters enormously.

This also explains why later changes to the monuments should be read carefully. Taking a position is canonically meaningful, but it does not magically transfer every ability, feat, or advantage possessed by the previous holder.
Upper Four vs. Lower Three: The Most Important Divide
One of the most useful ways to understand the list is to separate the upper four from the lower three.
The
Technique God, Dragon God, Fighting God, and Demon God
are tied to extraordinary beings, ancient history, unique bodies or equipment, and powers that sit outside normal expectations for even elite warriors.
The
Death God, Sword God, and North God
remain monstrous combatants, but their positions are easier to understand through recognizable martial concepts: sword technique, experience, deception, specialization, and adaptable tactics.
That does not mean every upper-rank fighter automatically defeats every lower-rank fighter in every situation. It means the narrative treats the top end as a particularly extreme tier.
Where Does Rudeus Fit Into the Seven Great Powers?
Rudeus is exactly why readers should distinguish
combat potential
from conventional warrior rankings.

His enormous mana capacity, voiceless casting, destructive magic, tactical intelligence, and later equipment let him threaten opponents who would annihilate most fighters. At the same time, his body does not naturally function like that of the setting’s greatest close-range warriors. Distance, preparation, armor, surprise, and information can radically change his odds.

Later in the light novel, Rudeus becomes directly relevant to the Seven Great Powers ranking. Explaining the exact change would add another major endgame spoiler, but the important point for power scaling is this:
his place in the hierarchy does not mean he suddenly becomes a superior pure duelist to every name below a given number.
His strength is unusually dependent on loadout and battle conditions.
The Seven Great Powers Ranked by Practical Threat
If we preserve the canonical monument order, the ranking is straightforward:
Technique God
Dragon God Orsted
Fighting God
Demon God Laplace
Death God Randolph Marianne
Sword God Gal Farion
North God Kalman III
For practical combat analysis, though,
Orsted deserves special treatment

. He has the broadest demonstrated package of combat tools among the major active fighters encountered in the story. Technique God remains No. 1 on the canonical ranking, but the text gives readers good reason not to reduce an Orsted-versus-Technique-God discussion to the numbers carved on a monument.

The same caution applies farther down. Gal can be lethal before a more versatile opponent gets started. Randolph becomes more dangerous when his enemy lacks information. Kalman III’s equipment and development can change the matchup. The Fighting God’s threat cannot be separated cleanly from the armor.
That complexity is a strength of
Mushoku Tensei’s
power system:
the list establishes status, while the battles establish context.
Why the Seven Great Powers Matter to Mushoku Tensei’s Worldbuilding

The Seven Great Powers do more than give fans a top-seven list. Early in Rudeus’s journey, the monuments communicate scale. They tell us that the protagonist, despite his exceptional magical talent, exists in a world with people and entities operating far beyond what he initially understands.

That changes how later encounters feel. Meeting a title like Dragon God is not simply meeting another strong adventurer. It means encountering someone whose name belongs to a centuries-old hierarchy recognized across the world.

The system also reinforces one of the series’ better approaches to strength: power is specialized. Swordsmanship, magic, equipment, racial abilities, experience, knowledge, and preparation can all produce different kinds of superiority. There is no single stat that explains every fight.
Readers following the anime toward its next major material can also see our
Mushoku Tensei Season 3 release date, story arcs, and details
guide for the adaptation side of the franchise.
Frequently Asked Questions
Who is No. 1 among the Seven Great Powers?
Technique God holds the No. 1 position in the established Seven Great Powers ranking.
Who is the Dragon God in Mushoku Tensei?
Orsted is the Dragon God and holds the No. 2 position when the ranking is introduced. He is one of the most formidable all-round combatants in the story.
Is Orsted stronger than the Technique God?

The canonical monuments rank Technique God first and Orsted second. A direct combat verdict is less certain than those numbers suggest because the ranking is not a perfect matchup calculator and Technique God’s full combat showing is limited.
Why is Laplace listed twice?
The original Demon Dragon God Laplace was divided, producing distinct halves associated with the Technique God and Demon God identities. That is why both titles are connected to Laplace.
Is Rudeus one of the Seven Great Powers?

Later light-novel events make Rudeus directly relevant to the ranking. The exact circumstances are a major spoiler. More importantly, his status should not be interpreted as proof that he automatically wins against every lower-ranked fighter in a neutral duel.
Can the Seven Great Powers ranking change?
Yes. The positions can change, and the monuments reflect changes in the recognized holders. This is why the list should always be tied to a specific point in the story.
Final Takeaway

Mushoku Tensei’s Seven Great Powers are best understood as a legendary, historically maintained hierarchy rather than a flawless spreadsheet of combat outcomes. The canonical order begins with Technique God at No. 1, followed by Orsted, Fighting God, Demon God, Death God, Sword God, and North God.

What makes the system interesting is everything the numbers leave out. Orsted’s versatility, the Fighting God Armor, Laplace’s divided nature, Randolph’s deception, Gal’s overwhelming offense, and Kalman III’s adaptability all show that strength in
Mushoku Tensei
is conditional.
The monuments tell you who belongs among the legends. The story tells you why a fight between legends can still be unpredictable.
