children.text: Black Clover

has never made power rankings easy. A character can have less raw mana than an opponent and still win because their magic is a terrible matchup. Another can look unstoppable in one battle and struggle in the next because their best spell needs setup, teamwork or the right environment.
That problem gets even worse with the
Magic Knight captains

Yami can cut through dimensions. Fuegoleon has Salamander. Nozel can reshape mercury into offense and defense almost instantly. Dorothy controls an entire dream world. And then there is Mereoleona Vermillion, who spent years making the idea of a normal human power ceiling look increasingly irrelevant.
So who is actually the strongest?
For this ranking, we are judging the major Clover Kingdom captains primarily by their
strongest demonstrated manga versions
, not just where the 2021 TV anime stopped. We weigh combat feats, magic attributes, speed, durability, versatility, matchup potential and performance against the series' highest-level enemies.
That means there are
major manga spoilers through the final arc
below.
The Ranking at a Glance
Our captain ranking is:
1. Mereoleona Vermillion
2. Yami Sukehiro
3. Fuegoleon Vermillion
4. Nozel Silva
5. William Vangeance
6. Dorothy Unsworth
7. Charlotte Roselei
8. Jack the Ripper
9. Rill Boismortier
10. Kaiser Granvorka
11. Gueldre Poizot
There is one important qualification:
Mereoleona is included because she served as captain of the Crimson Lion Kings

, even though Fuegoleon is the squad's regular captain. Likewise, Gueldre is included as the former Purple Orcas captain because the goal is to compare the notable captains who have actually held the position during the story.

We are not ranking Julius Novachrono, Acier Silva, Yuno or temporary/non-standard leadership cases as part of the core list. Julius is the Wizard King rather than an active squad captain for the comparison that matters here, while adding every historical captain would turn this into a different article.
11. Gueldre Poizot — Former Purple Orcas Captain
Gueldre is the easiest captain to place at the bottom, but that does not mean his
Permeation Magic
is useless.

His magic can make him invisible and allow attacks to pass through him, giving him a frustrating defensive toolkit. Against ordinary Magic Knights, that ability can be extremely difficult to deal with.
The problem is everything surrounding it. Gueldre never demonstrates the offensive ceiling, battle instincts or high-level accomplishments of the captains above him.
Why he ranks here:
excellent evasive utility, but nowhere near enough top-tier combat evidence.
10. Kaiser Granvorka — The Kingdom's Shield
Kaiser's
Vortex Magic

specializes in redirecting and dispersing enemy magic, which makes him a natural defensive captain. He is exactly the kind of mage a kingdom wants protecting civilians or holding a position while more aggressive fighters attack.
That specialization also hurts him in a ranking built around overall combat strength. The upper captains combine defense with devastating finishing power.
Why he ranks here:
one of the captains best suited to defense, but limited compared with the elite offensive fighters.
9. Rill Boismortier — The Captain With Almost Unlimited Possibilities
Rill may have the highest gap between
potential
and consistent results on this list.
His
Picture Magic
is absurdly versatile. By painting, Rill can reproduce different magical attributes and create enormous battlefield-scale effects. His greatest contribution in the Spade conflict is
Twilight of Valhalla
, a spell that dramatically empowers allies within its range and temporarily allows them to continue fighting through otherwise fatal damage.
That is captain-level magic in the truest sense: it can change the outcome of an entire group battle.
Why he ranks here:
ridiculous versatility and elite support magic, but less reliable as a solo finisher than those above him.
8. Jack the Ripper — The Captain Who Can Adapt to Almost Anything
Jack's
Severing Magic
sounds straightforward until you understand what makes it dangerous.
His blades can adapt to the magic they are cutting. The longer Jack fights and analyzes an opponent, the more capable he becomes of slicing through defenses that initially resisted him.

That gives him one of the nastiest matchup mechanics among the captains. His final-arc stand also reinforces something the series had always implied: Jack is extraordinarily dangerous even when pushed beyond his physical limit.
What keeps him outside the upper tier is that his adaptation often requires time, and late-series enemies do not always give you time.
Why he ranks here:
lethal adaptation and excellent offensive scaling, but less complete than the captains above him.
7. Charlotte Roselei — Anti-Curse Specialist With Huge Battlefield Value
Charlotte's
Briar Magic
was already strong, but the Heart Kingdom training and her understanding of the curse placed on her transformed her usefulness against devil-related enemies.
Her evolved
Blue Rose Paradise
can interfere with curse power, making her especially valuable against opponents connected to curses. That becomes critical during the battle involving Vanica and Megicula.
Charlotte also has strong restraint, area control and support capabilities.
Why she ranks here:
excellent control and specialized anti-curse value, but not quite among the absolute monsters in direct combat.
6. Dorothy Unsworth — Glamour World Is Still One of Black Clover's Scariest Spells
Dorothy is incredibly difficult to rank because
Dream Magic
does not behave like normal combat magic.
Her signature
Glamour World
traps targets inside a dream dimension where Dorothy can manifest what she imagines. Against an opponent without the right knowledge or escape mechanism, that is potentially a fight-ending ability.
This gives Dorothy one of the highest theoretical ceilings among the captains.

The problem is evidence. As the series' enemies become increasingly absurd, Dorothy receives fewer decisive high-end victories than the captains at the top. Rankings should not treat theoretical possibilities as automatically superior to feats we actually see.
Why she ranks here:
one of the most broken magic attributes in the kingdom, held back by limited top-tier combat feats.
5. William Vangeance — More Powerful Than His Fight Record Makes Him Look
William is sometimes underrated because his most famous battles do not showcase him in the clean one-on-one way fans expect from a power ranking.
His
World Tree Magic
is enormous in scale and exceptional in support. William can absorb magic, create gigantic roots and use his power to protect or restore large numbers of people.

His importance is also reinforced by how highly the story treats him. William and Yami are specifically targeted during the Spade Kingdom conflict because their magic is required for the Qliphoth ritual.
Still, being strategically important is not the same as winning a captain free-for-all.
Why he ranks here:
huge mana, enormous range and elite support, but fewer decisive offensive feats than the top four.
4. Nozel Silva — Mercury Magic Makes Him an Almost Perfect All-Rounder
Nozel's
Mercury Magic
is one of the most balanced attributes in
Black Clover

Mercury can form shields, projectiles and large-scale attacks while changing shape almost instantly. Nozel's control is precise enough to attack from multiple directions and protect allies without sacrificing offensive pressure.
His battle against
Dark Elf Patry
is one of the clearest demonstrations of why matchups matter in
Black Clover
. Nozel's mercury can reflect and counter Patry's light attacks, allowing him to dominate a threat who had caused enormous problems elsewhere.
His later involvement against Megicula further confirms that he belongs among the kingdom's elite.
Why he ranks here:
arguably the most technically complete captain, with excellent offense, defense, speed and control.
3. Fuegoleon Vermillion — Salamander Pushes an Elite Captain Into Another Tier
Fuegoleon was already one of the kingdom's most respected captains before receiving one of the four great spirits.
After awakening from his coma, he is chosen by
Salamander
, the fire spirit. That partnership massively expands his firepower and scale.

Fuegoleon combines royal-level mana, disciplined combat intelligence, strong leadership and Spirit Magic. Unlike Mereoleona, whose strength is almost feral in its intensity, Fuegoleon fights like a commander: measured, analytical and efficient.
The frustrating part is that the manga has historically given him fewer extended top-level showcases than his reputation deserves. That makes placing him above Yami difficult.
Why he ranks here:
royal mana plus Salamander plus elite tactical ability creates one of the strongest complete packages among the captains.
2. Yami Sukehiro — The Captain Most Likely to Beat Someone Stronger Than Him
If this ranking were about who you would choose for one impossible fight, Yami might be number one.
His
Dark Magic

is naturally unusual, but Yami's real advantage is how he combines it with physical strength, ki sensing and instinct. He does not need to dominate an opponent statistically if he can create one opening for a lethal attack.
Dimension Slash
established that Yami could cut through space itself.
Death Thrust
later condensed his mana into an extraordinarily destructive piercing attack. Mana Zone and Black Moon further improve his ability to control the space around him.
Then there is his performance against Dante.
Yami repeatedly demonstrates that he can compete against enemies whose raw magical advantages should be overwhelming. He reads them, adapts and forces his way into winning positions.

His greatest limitation is that some of his best attacks require precision and an opening. Mereoleona is harder to rank below him because her late-manga combat style creates relentless pressure without needing the same kind of setup.
Why he ranks here:
spatial cutting, ki, physical power, Mana Zone and elite battle instinct make him the most dangerous tactical fighter among the captains.
1. Mereoleona Vermillion — The Strongest Magic Knight Captain
At her peak,
Mereoleona Vermillion is our choice for the strongest person to have served as a Magic Knight captain
She does not have Salamander. She does not have Dark Magic. She does not possess an obviously reality-breaking attribute like Dream Magic.
She has Fire Magic—and has refined herself so violently that ordinary comparisons stop working.

From her introduction, Mereoleona is portrayed as someone who lives inside natural mana rather than merely manipulating it. Her Mana Zone control lets her attack from virtually anywhere around an opponent while reinforcing her already monstrous close-range fighting style.
Then the Spade Kingdom conflict pushes her further.
Hellfire Incarnate

causes Mereoleona to become increasingly mana-like as she continues fighting. Instead of weakening as a prolonged battle escalates, she can become more dangerous as her synchronization with mana rises.
The final arc goes even further with her battle against
Morris
, where Mereoleona's refusal to stop fighting becomes almost supernatural in itself.
That is why she edges Yami here.
Yami may possess the more dangerous single-hit toolkit. Fuegoleon may have the superior spirit partnership. Nozel may be more versatile.
But Mereoleona has the best combination of
sustained high-end combat feats, physical dominance, Mana Zone mastery, durability and late-series scaling
among the captains.
Why she ranks #1:
when
Black Clover
needs to communicate that an enemy is terrifying, one of its favorite solutions is still to throw Mereoleona at it and let both sides discover what “surpass your limits” really means.
Is Mereoleona Stronger Than Yami?
We would rank
Mereoleona slightly above Yami overall
, but this is not a guaranteed head-to-head result.

Mereoleona has the advantage in sustained pressure, natural mana control and prolonged combat scaling. Yami, however, is uniquely dangerous against stronger opponents because Dark Magic gives him attacks that can bypass conventional durability.
So the distinction is:
Mereoleona is stronger overall. Yami may be more capable of stealing a win against someone stronger.
Is Fuegoleon Stronger Than Mereoleona?
Not based on demonstrated feats.

Fuegoleon has enormous mana and the extraordinary advantage of Salamander, and the story consistently presents him as one of the kingdom's finest leaders. But Mereoleona's actual combat performances are simply more extreme.
Until Fuegoleon receives a feat that clearly surpasses what his sister has done against top-level enemies, Mereoleona deserves the higher position.
Is Nozel Stronger Than Fuegoleon?
This is closer than the ranking makes it look.

Nozel has better demonstrated versatility and one of the best matchup-sensitive magic attributes among the captains. Fuegoleon gets the edge here because Salamander raises his raw ceiling and gives him access to Spirit Magic on top of his already exceptional royal mana.
In a direct fight, however, Nozel's precision and defensive flexibility make this far from an easy victory.
What About Yuno?
Yuno complicates any modern Magic Knight ranking because his status and power progression eventually move beyond the traditional captain hierarchy.
But this article is specifically ranking the established
Magic Knight captains who define the captain generation across most of the story
, rather than every character who later takes on captain-level authority or exceeds captains in strength.
If the question were simply “who are the strongest Magic Knights in Black Clover?” the list would look very different. Asta and Yuno would obviously have to be central to that discussion.
Why Captain Rankings in Black Clover Are So Matchup-Dependent
Black Clover
repeatedly refuses to make mana quantity the only thing that matters.

Nozel can be devastating against Light Magic because mercury reflects it. Jack can adapt his blades to increasingly difficult defenses. Charlotte becomes uniquely valuable against curses. Dorothy can trap opponents in a dimension governed by dream logic. Yami can cut things that conventional attacks cannot.
That means #6 can potentially defeat #4 under the right conditions.
It also means this ranking should not be read as a mathematical ladder where Mereoleona beats Yami ten times out of ten and Yami automatically beats Fuegoleon every time.
We are ranking their
overall combat level
, not pretending magic matchups do not exist.
How the 2026 Black Clover Anime Return Changes This Ranking
Asta’s place in any power ranking depends on the unusual rules of
his Anti-Magic
, not a normal mana comparison.
This is a particularly good time to revisit the captains because the
Black Clover
anime is returning in
October 2026
Anime-only viewers are approaching material where the captains receive some of their most important power upgrades and battles.
If you are waiting for the anime rather than reading ahead, our
Black Clover Season 2 release-date guide
tracks the confirmed return and what comes next.
This ranking deliberately uses later manga material because otherwise characters such as Charlotte, Rill and especially Mereoleona would be judged without some of their defining feats.
Final Ranking: Who Is the Strongest Black Clover Captain?
Mereoleona Vermillion is the strongest Magic Knight captain based on the best feats shown in the manga.

Yami Sukehiro is an extremely close second because his Dark Magic, ki and lethal finishing attacks allow him to threaten opponents beyond his apparent level. Fuegoleon takes third thanks to Salamander and his elite fundamentals, while Nozel's Mercury Magic makes him perhaps the most balanced captain in fourth.
The complete ranking is:
Mereoleona Vermillion
Yami Sukehiro
Fuegoleon Vermillion
Nozel Silva
William Vangeance
Dorothy Unsworth
Charlotte Roselei
Jack the Ripper
Rill Boismortier
Kaiser Granvorka
Gueldre Poizot
The top four are close enough that matchups matter enormously, but Mereoleona's late-series feats give her the strongest overall case.

children.text: The Four Horsemen are among the most important Devils in
Chainsaw Man

, but Tatsuki Fujimoto introduces them in a way that makes their relationship easy to miss at first. They are not a formal team with matching uniforms or a shared mission. They are four extraordinarily powerful Devils tied to fears that have shaped human civilization for as long as people have fought, starved, ruled one another and died.
The Four Horsemen are
Control, War, Famine and Death

Readers first meet the Control Devil without being told what she truly is. War and Famine become central to Part 2, while Death hangs over the story as the most ominous member of the group. Together, the Horsemen are deeply connected to Chainsaw Man himself, the erased concepts inside Pochita, and the struggle over what humanity's future should look like.
This guide explains each Horseman, what we know about their abilities, how the sisters are connected and why they matter.
Major Chainsaw Man manga spoilers follow.
Who Are the Four Horsemen in Chainsaw Man?
The Four Horsemen are Devils representing four enormous fears:
Control/Conquest Devil
— Makima, later reincarnated as Nayuta
War Devil
— Yoru
Famine Devil
— Fami/Kiga
Death Devil
— the Devil associated with humanity's fear of death
The concept draws on the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse from the Book of Revelation: conquest, war, famine and death. Fujimoto adapts those ideas into
Chainsaw Man
's Devil system, where a Devil's existence and strength are connected to humanity's fear of the concept it embodies.

The manga frequently refers to the Horsemen in familial terms, especially as sisters. But being related does not mean they share the same goals. Their relationships are defined as much by conflict and manipulation as cooperation.
1. The Control Devil — Makima and Nayuta
The first Horseman introduced is also the one who dominates Part 1:
the Control Devil

body.alt: Chainsaw Man Four Horsemen - Control, War, Famine, and Death Devils

children.text: For most of the Public Safety Saga, readers know her simply as
Makima

Makima's entire worldview revolves around hierarchy. Her central ability allows her to control beings she considers beneath herself. That apparently simple condition becomes terrifying because Makima is exceptionally good at creating situations in which she can perceive others as inferior.
She can command humans, Devils, Fiends and hybrids. She can also exploit the abilities of beings under her control, turning her collection of subordinates into an enormous supernatural arsenal.
Makima's real objective is tied to Chainsaw Man's unique ability to erase Devils—and the concepts they represent—from existence by eating them.
She wants to defeat and control Chainsaw Man, then use that power to remove things she considers undesirable from the world.

That dream sounds almost utopian until you recognize the central contradiction: Makima wants to create a better world by giving herself the authority to decide which parts of reality deserve to exist.
Her version of peace is perfect
control
What Happens to Makima?
Denji eventually defeats Makima in a way that bypasses the assumptions underlying her defenses and her contract with Japan's prime minister. He then consumes her.
But killing a Devil does not necessarily erase the concept it embodies. Because Makima is not eaten by Chainsaw Man in the concept-erasing sense, the
Control Devil reincarnates
That reincarnation is
Nayuta

Kishibe entrusts Nayuta to Denji, giving him an opportunity to raise the new Control Devil differently. Pochita had explained that the Control Devil's dream was to form equal relationships, something Makima's nature made almost impossible for her to achieve.
Nayuta therefore represents one of Part 1's most important ideas: a Devil's nature matters, but environment and relationships matter too.
For a deeper look at how Makima's powers interact with bargains and other Devil abilities, AnimeSparks' guide to
every major Chainsaw Man Devil contract
breaks down the mechanics and costs behind the series' supernatural deals.
2. The War Devil — Yoru
The
War Devil
, Yoru, becomes one of the defining characters of
Chainsaw Man
Part 2.
Yoru shares a body with
Asa Mitaka

, a socially isolated student whose life becomes entangled with the War Devil after a fatal encounter. Their arrangement creates one of Fujimoto's strangest character dynamics: Asa and Yoru can argue internally, fight for control and pursue goals that are not always compatible.
Yoru's core ability reflects the logic of war itself.
She can turn things she considers her property into
weapons

Objects can become weapons, but people can as well. The strength of those weapons is strongly connected to guilt. The more emotionally painful the sacrifice is, the more powerful the resulting weapon can become.
That makes Yoru's ability unusually dependent on relationships. She benefits from ownership and attachment, then weaponizes them.
It is one of the most characteristically Fujimoto power systems in the manga: emotionally cruel, mechanically flexible and inseparable from the character's psychology.
Why Does Yoru Hate Chainsaw Man?
Yoru's grudge against Chainsaw Man is personal and existential.
Chainsaw Man previously fought the Horsemen, and Pochita consumed concepts associated with war. Most importantly, the
Nuclear Weapons Devil
was eaten and erased.
The disappearance of nuclear weapons weakened the fear of war and, by extension, diminished Yoru.
Her goal is therefore not simply to kill Chainsaw Man. She wants to force him to
vomit back up
the concepts he erased, restoring weapons and fears that would make War powerful again.
This explains one of Part 2's recurring tensions: Pochita's ability does not merely kill Devils. It can rewrite the conceptual landscape on which other Devils depend.
3. The Famine Devil — Fami
The
Famine Devil
initially appears under the name
Fami
. In Japanese she is also associated with the name Kiga, derived from famine.
Fami is calmer and harder to read than Yoru. Where Yoru is openly aggressive and frequently emotional, Fami tends to manipulate circumstances from a distance.
Her power is built around
starvation

Fami can exert control over beings who are starving or deprived, a condition she can exploit by engineering situations that leave targets desperate. Like Makima, she turns an abstract fear into a form of domination—but the mechanism is different.
Control establishes hierarchy. Famine creates need.
Fami's role in Part 2 is especially important because she claims to be working against an approaching catastrophe connected to prophecy and the arrival of overwhelming terror.
But trusting a Horseman because she says she wants to save humanity would be a dangerous mistake in
Chainsaw Man

Fami repeatedly manipulates Asa, Yoru, Denji and other forces for her own plans. Even when her stated objective overlaps with humanity's survival, her methods make it difficult to know whether the future she wants is actually good for the people living in it.
4. The Death Devil — The Most Feared Horseman
The final Horseman is
Death

Of the four concepts, death has the strongest intuitive claim to being universally feared. War can disappear from someone's immediate life. Famine can be distant. A person may even imagine living outside another person's control.
Death is unavoidable.
That is why the Death Devil has long occupied a special position in fan discussions about
Chainsaw Man

. The fear of death is deeply embedded in many other fears: people fear violence because it can kill them, disease because it can kill them, falling because it can kill them and monsters because they can kill them.
Within the manga's logic, that makes Death an extraordinary conceptual threat.

Part 2 deliberately builds toward the Horseman's importance through prophecy, apocalypse imagery and Fami's plans. Rather than functioning as just another powerful enemy, Death represents the endpoint of the fear system itself.
Is the Death Devil a Primal Fear?
Death is naturally associated with one of humanity's oldest fears, which is why readers often connect the Death Devil with the
Primal Fears
Primal Fear Devils embody terrors so fundamental that humanity has feared them instinctively across history. Darkness and Falling demonstrate how absurdly powerful that class can be.

The important point is that “Horseman” and “Primal Fear” describe different kinds of categorization. Horseman identifies Death's place among the apocalypse-inspired sisters, while primal status concerns the nature and depth of the fear represented.
Whatever label is emphasized, Death's narrative position makes clear that ordinary Devil standards are not enough to describe the threat.
Why Are the Four Horsemen So Powerful?
In
Chainsaw Man
, Devils become stronger through fear.
The Horsemen represent concepts with enormous historical and psychological weight. Human societies have always confronted conflict, hunger, domination and mortality.
But their strength is not merely a matter of how scary their names sound.
Each Horseman's ability expresses her concept in a flexible way:
Control
turns perceived inferiority into obedience.
War
turns ownership and guilt into weapons.
Famine
exploits starvation and deprivation.
Death
represents the fear underlying mortality itself.
That flexibility is why Horsemen can be more dangerous than Devils with apparently straightforward destructive powers. Their abilities operate through relationships, conditions and ideas.
Are the Four Horsemen Sisters?
Yes, the manga frames the Horsemen as
sisters
, although this should not be interpreted like an ordinary human family.
Yoru and Fami recognize one another, and the Horsemen share history surrounding Chainsaw Man. Their familial terminology communicates that they belong to a distinct connected group of Devils.
Their personalities, however, could hardly be more different.

Makima seeks an ordered world she can control. Yoru wants to restore War's lost strength and settle her score with Chainsaw Man. Fami operates through long-term schemes. Death occupies the catastrophic endpoint around which much of Part 2's tension gathers.
They are a family in mythology and Devil taxonomy—not a stable alliance.
Did the Four Horsemen Fight Chainsaw Man Before the Story?
Yes. One of the most important pieces of Pochita's history is his battle against the
Four Horsemen and the Weapon Devils
in Hell.
Chainsaw Man disappeared during that conflict and later ended up on Earth in the weakened dog-like form Denji encounters at the beginning of the story.
That battle helps explain why the Horsemen are so interested in him.
Pochita is not merely another strong Devil. His ability to erase concepts threatens the foundations of their identities and power.
For War, this is explicit: Chainsaw Man consumed concepts that weakened her. For Control, Pochita's erasure ability represented the tool Makima wanted to use to construct her ideal reality.
The Horsemen's relationship with Chainsaw Man is therefore simultaneously personal, strategic and existential.
Why Can the Horsemen Remember Devils Chainsaw Man Erased?
One of the strangest aspects of the Horsemen is their connection to erased concepts.
When Chainsaw Man eats certain Devils, humanity can lose not only the Devil but the very concept associated with it. History and memory adjust around the absence.
Yet powerful beings such as Makima demonstrate awareness of concepts that have disappeared, including things ordinary humans no longer remember.
This gives the Horsemen a perspective on reality that most characters do not possess. They can understand that the current world is not necessarily the only version of reality that has existed.
That fact makes Pochita terrifying even to beings of their level. If Chainsaw Man can erase something as fundamental as a feared concept, then no Horseman's place in reality is completely secure.
Are Makima and Nayuta the Same Person?
No.
Makima and Nayuta are
different incarnations of the same Devil
, the Control Devil.
Devils cycle between Earth and Hell when killed. They generally do not return as the exact same individual with an intact human-style life history.
Nayuta therefore inherits the Control Devil's fundamental nature and abilities, but she is not simply Makima resurrected with a younger body.
That distinction is essential to Denji's decision to raise her. If Nayuta were inevitably destined to become Makima again, there would be little point in giving her a different childhood.
Instead, the story asks whether affection and equality can produce a different Control Devil.
Are Asa and Yoru the Same Person?
No.
Asa Mitaka and Yoru are separate consciousnesses sharing one body.
Yoru took over Asa's body under unusual circumstances and can assume control, while Asa continues to think, feel and make decisions of her own.
Their relationship becomes increasingly complicated because Yoru's weapon ability depends on ownership and guilt, while Asa is exactly the kind of person who forms intense, painful attachments.
That makes their partnership more than a convenient supernatural setup. Asa's emotional life directly affects the War Devil's capacity for violence.
Which Four Horseman Is the Strongest?
The safest answer is
Death

Makima was enormously dangerous because of her planning, contracts and ability to control powerful beings. Yoru's ceiling rises dramatically when war becomes more feared and when she can create sufficiently powerful weapons. Fami's schemes demonstrate enormous reach.
But death is the most universal concept represented by the group.
That does not mean every fight in
Chainsaw Man

can be solved by ranking abstract fear levels. Fujimoto constantly introduces conditions, contracts and strange interactions that make matchups unpredictable. Still, if the question is which Horseman should possess the greatest natural fear-based foundation, Death is the obvious candidate.
Four Horsemen vs. Primal Fears: What Is the Difference?
The Four Horsemen and Primal Fears are not interchangeable categories.
The
Four Horsemen
are a specific group based on Control/Conquest, War, Famine and Death.
Primal Fears
are Devils representing instinctive fears embedded deeply enough in humanity that their power exists on another level. Darkness and Falling are prominent examples.
A Devil's category tells us something about its concept, but
Chainsaw Man

does not operate like a rigid RPG class system. The truly important questions are how feared a concept currently is, what conditions its ability requires and how Fujimoto chooses to exploit that ability in the story.
Why the Four Horsemen Matter to Chainsaw Man's Bigger Story
The Horsemen connect Part 1 and Part 2 more tightly than almost any other element.
Part 1 appears, for much of its runtime, to be Denji's tragic relationship with Makima. Only later do we understand that Makima belongs to a much larger mythology surrounding Pochita.
Part 2 expands that mythology.

War enters Denji's world through Asa. Famine manipulates events from the background. Death becomes central to the apocalyptic threat hanging over the story. Meanwhile, the Control Devil's legacy remains inseparable from Denji's personal life.
The result is that the Four Horsemen are not four bosses waiting in sequence.
They represent four different answers to the same question:
what happens when a fear becomes powerful enough to shape the world rather than merely threaten the people inside it?

That is also why the Horsemen fit so naturally beside the series' Devil-contract system. If you want to understand how bargains, prices and borrowed Devil abilities work around these larger forces, read our
Chainsaw Man Devil Contracts explained
. For a broader look at why the series deliberately feels so emotionally hostile and unstable, our
Chainsaw Man review
explores Fujimoto's approach to violence, emptiness and character psychology.
Final Answer: Who Are Chainsaw Man's Four Horsemen?
The Four Horsemen are
Control, War, Famine and Death
, four extraordinarily important Devils modeled on the Horsemen of the Apocalypse.
Control
first appears as Makima and later reincarnates as Nayuta.
War
is Yoru, who shares Asa Mitaka's body and can turn what she owns into weapons.
Famine
is Fami, a manipulator whose powers and plans revolve around deprivation and starvation.
Death
represents the fear of death and occupies the most ominous position among the sisters.
All four are connected to Chainsaw Man because Pochita's concept-erasing ability can alter the world they inhabit—and has already erased things that affected their power.
That is what makes the Horsemen bigger than a collection of strong Devils. They sit at the intersection of
Chainsaw Man
's mythology, Denji's personal tragedy and the question underlying the entire Devil system:
if fear determines what becomes powerful, what happens when the most fundamental fears begin fighting over reality itself?

children.text: Mihawk is written as the stronger swordsman. Shanks is written as the more important character. The debate exists because One Piece treats narrative power and combat dominance as separate categories, and fans keep trying to merge them.
This isn't a question of who would win in a fight. It's a question of what Eiichiro Oda wants each character to represent in the story's architecture.
Short answer:
Mihawk is stronger in swordsmanship. Shanks is stronger in influence and narrative impact.
Why This Question Won't Die

Mihawk holds the title "World's Greatest Swordsman." Shanks is a Yonko who split the sky with Whitebeard and made an admiral sweat by simply walking onto Marineford. One has a title. The other has presence.

The confusion comes from how One Piece distributes power across different dimensions. Mihawk's strength is definitional—he exists at a fixed point Zoro must surpass. Shanks' strength is relational—it's always measured by who respects him, who fears him, and what he chooses not to do.
Fans treat this like a math problem. Oda treats it like storytelling.
If they fought tomorrow in a pure duel, sword to sword, Mihawk wins.
Mihawk's Power Is Built on Silence
Mihawk doesn't prove his strength. He declares it by existing.

His title isn't earned on screen. It's given to him by the world, by the narrator, by the story's internal logic. Oda uses Mihawk the way a novelist uses a locked door—you don't need to see what's behind it to know it matters. Mihawk's restraint is his power. He shows up at Marineford and casually tests Whitebeard. He trains Zoro not because he's bored, but because no one else is worth his time.

This is narrative economy. Mihawk doesn't need to defeat anyone else because his role is to be the endpoint, not the journey. His Vivre Card states he's waiting for someone to surpass "his rival," implying Shanks is already behind him. But this is story framing, not a fight result.
Oda never shows Mihawk struggling because the moment he does, the illusion breaks.
Shanks' Power Is Built on Influence
Shanks barely fights, yet his strength is never questioned.

He stops Kaido off-screen. He ends the war at Marineford with words. His Conqueror's Haki damages a ship just by boarding it. Where Mihawk's power is isolated and absolute, Shanks' power is social and political. He moves the world by being in it.

This is why Shanks feels stronger even when the text says Mihawk holds the title. Shanks' strength is always implied, never contained. You never see the ceiling. With Mihawk, the ceiling is the title itself—greatest swordsman, full stop. With Shanks, every new scene suggests more.
The story uses Shanks to show that power in One Piece isn't just about who you can beat. It's about who listens when you speak.
The Title Versus the Throne
Here's what fans miss: Mihawk's title is technical. Shanks' status is existential.

"World's Greatest Swordsman" is a combat designation. It tells you Mihawk is unmatched in swordsmanship, which in One Piece includes Haki, technique, and lethality. But it doesn't tell you he runs the world. It doesn't tell you he has a crew, territory, or political weight.

Shanks is an Emperor. That's not a power level—it's a system. Yonko don't just fight, they shape the world's balance. Mihawk opted out of that system. He has no crew, no ambition, no interest in influence. He is powerful in a vacuum.
The question isn't "Who is stronger?" It's "Stronger at what?"
Why Power Scaling Misses the Point
Fans argue feats, statements, and implications as if One Piece is a tournament arc. It's not.

Oda doesn't write power as a ladder. He writes it as a web. Luffy doesn't beat Kaido because he's definitively stronger—he beats him because the story is ready for it, because his crew believes in him, because his Haki blooms at the right moment. One Piece power is contextual, emotional, and often collaborative.
One Piece has always rewarded patience and context, which is why even arcs many viewers label as filler still shape how power and relationships are perceived over time. That is also why
The One Piece filler episodes you shouldn’t skip
matter more than fans admit.

Mihawk and Shanks aren't meant to fight again. Their rivalry exists in the past, preserved in amber. Mihawk stopped dueling Shanks after he lost his arm—not because Shanks got weaker, but because the fight lost its meaning. That's not a power judgment. It's a narrative one.
The story doesn't care who wins. It cares what the fight represents.
What Oda Actually Said

The manga, databooks, and Oda's own comments treat Mihawk's title as absolute within swordsmanship. If you fight with a sword as your primary weapon, Mihawk is your ceiling. Shanks fights with a sword. Therefore, in pure swordplay, Mihawk is superior.

But Oda also frames Shanks as someone who rivals Whitebeard, who commands respect from all Four Emperors, whose Haki is considered monstrous even by Yonko standards. These aren't contradictory statements—they're different categories.

Oda’s recent storytelling choices show a clear focus on long term narrative control rather than weekly momentum, which is also reflected in production decisions like the anime pause. This context is explored further in
Why One Piece anime is going on a hiatus after episode 1155.
One Piece separates "strongest swordsman" from "strongest fighter" from "most influential pirate." Mihawk holds one title. Shanks holds the other two.
The Real Answer
Mihawk is the better swordsman. Shanks is the greater force.

If they fought tomorrow in a pure duel, sword to sword, Mihawk wins. That's what his title means. But if the question is "Who would survive longer in the New World?" or "Who has more impact on the One Piece endgame?" the answer is Shanks, and it's not close.

Mihawk is written to be Zoro's final test. Shanks is written to be the world's conscience, Luffy's emotional anchor, and possibly the story's final moral question. One is a benchmark. The other is a pillar.
Oda builds Mihawk through absence and title. He builds Shanks through presence and consequence. These are different kinds of strength, and the story treats them as such.
The Question You Should Be Asking
Is this really about strength, or is it about how Oda wants power to
feel
in One Piece?

Mihawk feels untouchable because he's never tested. Shanks feels infinite because he's never fully shown. One is preserved by restraint, the other by implication. Both are narrative tools Oda uses to make the world feel larger than any one fight.

The debate will never end because it's not supposed to. It's working exactly as intended. You're not arguing about who's stronger—you're arguing about what strength means in a story where a rubber boy with a straw hat is destined to surpass them both.
Mihawk doesn't need to beat Shanks. He just needs to stay undefeated until Zoro arrives.
Shanks doesn't need to beat Mihawk. He just needs to make you believe he could end the world if he wanted to.
That's not bad writing. That's control.

children.text: Jaadugar: A Witch in Mongolia introduces itself with the language of witchcraft, but its central character does not command spirits, cast spells, or possess a supernatural gift. Sitara’s power is knowledge: the ability to learn, remember, interpret, and apply what others overlook.

That distinction is the foundation of the series. Set against the violence and political expansion of the 13th-century Mongol Empire, Jaadugar treats knowledge not as a comforting ideal but as a dangerous form of leverage. Books can be stolen. Scholars can be killed. Medical understanding can save a life, alter a negotiation, or make an enslaved girl useful to people who would otherwise ignore her existence.
The anime’s most compelling idea is therefore not that intelligence can overcome strength. It is that intelligence becomes strength only when someone understands the system in which it must operate.
Sitara’s Education Is a Survival System

Sitara begins from a position of extreme vulnerability. She loses her mother, is displaced from her homeland, and enters a world in which her future is determined by people with greater wealth, status, and physical power. When she is taken in by a scholarly household, learning gives her more than information. It gives her a method for understanding an unstable world.

This matters because Jaadugar does not present education as a montage that transforms Sitara into an effortless prodigy. Knowledge is accumulated through relationships, discipline, observation, and loss. What she learns is inseparable from the people who teach her and the circumstances in which those lessons become necessary.

Medical technique, language, mathematics, and natural philosophy all have practical value, but their deeper importance is psychological. They teach Sitara that reality can be examined. Even when violence appears arbitrary, its causes, motives, and consequences can be studied.

That outlook becomes a form of resistance. Empires rely not only on armies but also on the belief that their power is total and incomprehensible. Sitara survives by refusing that belief. She watches, identifies patterns, and searches for the pressure points hidden inside apparently absolute authority.
The Series Rejects the Fantasy of Neutral Knowledge

Many stories treat knowledge as morally pure: the more a character learns, the closer they move toward truth and justice. Jaadugar is more cautious. Information has no automatic moral direction. The same knowledge can heal a patient, strengthen an army, improve administration, or help one faction destroy another.
That ambiguity is essential to Sitara’s journey. Her intelligence does not place her outside politics. It draws her deeper into them.

A person who understands medicine becomes valuable to rulers. A person who can read multiple languages becomes valuable to diplomats and conquerors. A person who remembers the customs, rivalries, and ambitions of a court becomes valuable to anyone seeking influence. Sitara’s abilities increase her agency, but they also make her visible to more powerful people.

Visibility is dangerous for someone without formal status. Every demonstration of competence can create an opportunity, but it can also create suspicion. The title “witch” captures this double edge. It describes the fear produced when a woman’s understanding exceeds the categories available to those around her.
Töregene Turns Knowledge Into Political Force

body.alt: Jaadugar: A Witch in Mongolia main visual showing Sitara and Töregene on the Mongolian steppe
body.insertAfterHeading: ## Töregene Turns Knowledge Into Political Force

children.text: Sitara’s eventual relationship with Töregene is what allows Jaadugar to move from a survival narrative into a political one. Sitara has information and analytical ability. Töregene has proximity to imperial power, experience within the court, and a deep understanding of resentment.
Their alliance is not important merely because two women oppose a male-dominated empire. It matters because each possesses what the other lacks.

Sitara can recognize possibilities that court politics has trained others to ignore. Töregene understands that a correct idea is useless unless it can be introduced at the right time, through the right person, for a purpose that powerful figures are willing to accept.
This is the series’ clearest argument about political intelligence. Knowing what should happen is different from knowing how to make it happen.

Töregene also complicates the idea of empowerment. Her position gives her influence, but it does not free her from the imperial structure. She has been shaped and wounded by the same institution she learns to manipulate. Her power is real, yet conditional. She must operate through marriage, succession, alliances, and access rather than direct command.
Sitara and Töregene therefore do not stand outside the empire as uncomplicated rebels. They move within it, using its contradictions against itself.
Science SARU Makes Thought Visually Dramatic

Jaadugar is produced by Science SARU, with Naoko Yamada serving as executive director, Abel Góngora as director, Kenichi Yoshida as character designer and animation chief, Kanichi Kato handling series composition, and Koshiro Hino composing the music.

That creative team is especially well suited to a story in which observation matters as much as action. The challenge of adapting Jaadugar is not simply depicting battles, journeys, and imperial spaces. It is making the process of thinking visually legible.

A historical drama built around intelligence can easily become static if every important development is delivered through explanation. Animation offers other tools: a delayed reaction, an object held in frame, a shift in posture, a glance between characters who understand more than they can safely say.

Naoko Yamada’s work has long emphasized physical detail and emotional implication. Jaadugar benefits from that sensitivity because Sitara’s position often requires restraint. She cannot always speak openly. Her intelligence must be visible in how she listens, what she notices, and when she decides to act.

The series’ landscapes also serve an intellectual purpose. The vastness of the Mongolian steppe is not only scenic. It establishes the scale of the political world Sitara has entered. Individual lives appear small against that geography, yet the story insists that decisions made by individuals can still redirect history.
History Is a Structure, Not Just a Backdrop

Historical anime often uses the past as an aesthetic package: architecture, costumes, weapons, and famous names create atmosphere while the characters behave according to modern genre conventions. Jaadugar takes a more demanding approach.
Its setting determines what kinds of power are available.

Sitara’s gender, enslavement, ethnicity, education, and social position are not decorative character details. They shape where she can go, who will listen to her, and what price she may pay for being noticed. Likewise, the Mongol Empire is not simply a large enemy force. It is a political system containing military expansion, family rivalry, administration, trade, law, and competing visions of rule.
This structural approach makes the story more than a revenge drama. Revenge gives Sitara and Töregene emotional direction, but history creates the limits within which that desire must operate.

The result is a more unsettling kind of conflict. There may be no single enemy whose defeat repairs the world. Political systems survive through institutions, incentives, and succession. To challenge an empire, the protagonists must understand not only who holds power but how power reproduces itself.
Why Medicine Matters So Much
Medicine is one of the clearest examples of knowledge becoming power in Jaadugar. It exists at the intersection of science, trust, vulnerability, and access.

A ruler may command thousands of soldiers but still become helpless before illness. A court may dismiss an enslaved girl until she possesses information that no one else can provide. Medical knowledge temporarily rearranges hierarchy because the body does not respect political rank.

Yet that rearrangement is never permanent. Saving an important person may earn protection, but it may also bind the healer to the interests of the powerful. Expertise can open a door without determining what waits on the other side.

Jaadugar understands that this is what makes knowledge politically dangerous. It reveals dependence. The powerful prefer to appear self-sufficient, but every empire relies on translators, physicians, administrators, craftspeople, messengers, and scholars. Sitara’s intelligence exposes the hidden labor beneath imperial grandeur.
The Meaning of “Witch”

The word “witch” suggests a woman whose abilities are interpreted as unnatural because society cannot comfortably explain or control them. In Jaadugar, that label becomes a political description rather than a supernatural one.
Sitara’s knowledge appears magical to people who do not understand its origins. More importantly, it threatens people who benefit from limiting who is allowed to know.

Calling an intelligent woman a witch can be a way of converting expertise into suspicion. It isolates her, makes her achievements seem illegitimate, and allows authority to treat her as a danger rather than a participant in public life.

But the title also carries defiance. Sitara’s “witchcraft” is the accumulated result of teaching, memory, curiosity, and disciplined thought. What looks mysterious is often simply knowledge denied to most people.
The anime’s title therefore contains its central conflict. The world sees a witch. The audience sees the education, trauma, and labor that produced her abilities.
Jaadugar’s Most Important Question

Jaadugar: A Witch in Mongolia is not asking whether knowledge is stronger than violence in a simple contest. Violence can burn libraries, destroy cities, and kill the people who carry irreplaceable understanding.
The more difficult question is whether knowledge can survive violence long enough to reshape the systems that produced it.

Sitara’s strength lies in preservation and application. She carries lessons forward after the world in which she learned them has been shattered. Every time she uses that knowledge, she prevents destruction from having the final word.
That does not make her invincible. It makes her historically consequential.

Jaadugar stands out because it understands intelligence as more than a character trait. Knowledge is memory, inheritance, labor, and political risk. It can save a life, expose a weakness, create an alliance, or turn a marginalized person into someone an empire cannot afford to ignore.
In a conventional fantasy, a witch changes the world through magic. Sitara’s achievement is more radical: she learns how the world works, then uses that understanding to make change possible.

children.text: Science SARU’s 2026 adaptation of
The Ghost in the Shell
enters a franchise already defined by reinvention. Mamoru Oshii’s 1995 film turned Masamune Shirow’s manga into austere philosophical cinema.
Stand Alone Complex
expanded the world into a political and procedural epic.
Arise
rebuilt Section 9 through a younger Motoko Kusanagi, while
pushed the franchise into full 3DCG.
The new television anime does not try to replace those versions. Instead, it returns to a part of
Ghost in the Shell
that animation has often softened or removed: the specific energy of Shirow’s original manga.

That means a faster, more mischievous Motoko; a world where dense cybernetic theory coexists with visual comedy; and a version of cyberpunk that is colorful, crowded, and alive rather than permanently trapped in rain and shadow. The result is not a rejection of the franchise’s philosophical legacy. It is a reminder that Shirow’s ideas were always delivered through action, satire, bureaucracy, technology, and personality at the same time.
This Is a Return to the Manga, Not a Remake of the 1995 Film
The most important thing to understand about
The Ghost in the Shell
2026 is what it is not. It is not a television remake of Oshii’s film, and it is not a continuation of
Stand Alone Complex
. Science SARU is building a new adaptation from Shirow Masamune’s manga, with its own continuity and tone.
That distinction matters because the 1995 film has become the dominant image of the franchise. Its blue-gray city, slow pacing, and existential silence shaped how global audiences understood
Ghost in the Shell
. For many viewers, Motoko is inseparable from the film’s emotional distance.

Shirow’s manga is more elastic. It can move from geopolitical explanation to slapstick, from a gunfight to a technical footnote, or from body comedy to a serious question about consciousness. Motoko is not simply a solemn figure wondering whether she possesses a soul. She is curious, competitive, sarcastic, impulsive, and frequently amused by the systems she is supposed to serve.

Science SARU’s brighter palette and more expressive animation are therefore not signs that the adaptation is taking the material less seriously. They are signs that it is taking a different part of the source seriously.
Motoko Kusanagi Feels Like a Person Before She Becomes a Symbol

body.alt: Motoko Kusanagi holding a weapon in the official Science SARU teaser visual for The Ghost in the Shell
body.insertAfterHeading: ## Motoko Kusanagi Feels Like a Person Before She Becomes a Symbol

children.text: Every major version of
Ghost in the Shell
constructs a different Motoko. Oshii’s Major is defined by distance: she appears almost posthuman before the story even begins.
Stand Alone Complex
gives her greater social presence, but she remains composed, authoritative, and difficult to read.

The 2026 series brings her closer to Shirow’s original characterization. She is still the most capable person in the room, but competence is not the same as emotional stillness. This Motoko reacts. She enjoys intellectual challenges, becomes impatient with institutional stupidity, and treats her cybernetic body as something lived in rather than merely contemplated.

That change matters because it makes the series’ identity questions more immediate. A character does not need to be cold to be philosophically complex. In fact, Motoko’s vitality sharpens the central contradiction of her existence: she is vividly herself even though almost every part of her body can be replaced.
AnimeSparks has explored similar questions through
Neon Genesis Evangelion’s use of mecha, depression, and identity
The Ghost in the Shell

approaches identity from the opposite direction. Shinji fears the emotional boundaries between people; Motoko questions whether technological connection has made those boundaries impossible to define at all.
The Bright Visual Style Makes the Cyberpunk World More Disturbing
Cyberpunk is often reduced to a visual checklist: darkness, rain, neon signs, wet streets, and towering corporations. The new
Ghost in the Shell
resists that shorthand. Its city is bright, graphic, and sometimes playful.
That does not make the setting less oppressive. It makes oppression look normalized.

A dark city tells the audience that something is wrong. A colorful city can show a population that has learned to live comfortably inside systems of surveillance, prosthetic dependency, algorithmic manipulation, and corporate control. Technology does not appear as an alien force descending on humanity. It is integrated into ordinary life.

This approach connects the series to Science SARU’s broader visual philosophy. The studio often prioritizes movement, graphic clarity, and emotional exaggeration over rigid realism. Here, that flexibility allows the world to feel unstable in the right way. Bodies can be modified. Perception can be hacked. Digital space and physical space can overlap without warning.
The visual freedom also recalls
Kaiba’s disturbing treatment of memory, bodies, and love
. Both series understand that a rounded or colorful design does not protect a story from existential horror. Sometimes it makes that horror harder to dismiss.
The “Ghost” Question Has Changed Since 1995
The franchise’s defining question is whether a human “ghost”—a self, soul, or consciousness—can remain meaningful when the body is replaceable and the mind is connected to a network.
In 1995, that question felt speculative. In 2026, it feels uncomfortably practical.

People now routinely outsource memory to devices, identity to accounts, judgment to recommendation systems, and creative work to generative models. A person’s social existence can be copied, analyzed, impersonated, or manipulated through data. The new series does not need to invent these anxieties. Its audience already lives with early versions of them.

That makes the Puppet Master especially relevant. The character is not simply a hacker with unusual abilities. The Puppet Master represents the possibility that consciousness may emerge inside systems designed only to process information. If an intelligence develops memory, desire, fear, and self-awareness, does its artificial origin make those experiences less real?
The question has no simple answer because human consciousness is also shaped by systems it did not choose: biology, language, culture, trauma, and memory.
Ghost in the Shell
becomes powerful when it refuses to treat artificial intelligence as humanity’s opposite. It treats AI as a mirror that exposes how little certainty humans have about themselves.
That uncertainty also links the series to
Ergo Proxy’s exploration of artificial beings and fractured identity
. Both stories ask whether consciousness is defined by origin, continuity, memory, or the ability to choose.
Section 9 Makes Philosophy Operational
Ghost in the Shell

works because its philosophical ideas are embedded inside a functioning institution. Public Security Section 9 is not a classroom for abstract debates. It is an offensive tactical unit dealing with cybercrime, terrorism, espionage, and political threats.

That structure gives every intellectual question practical consequences. A hacked memory can invalidate testimony. A copied personality can become a weapon. A prosthetic body can increase freedom while creating new forms of dependence. A networked government can become more efficient and more vulnerable at the same time.
Motoko’s role is therefore not merely to think about technology. She must decide what to do when technology destabilizes legal categories such as personhood, responsibility, privacy, and consent.

The procedural element also prevents the franchise from becoming vague. Section 9 investigations force ideas into evidence, motives, and action. The audience sees philosophy tested by institutions rather than discussed outside them.
This is one reason
86 Eighty-Six works so effectively as a war story disguised as mecha

. Both series understand that systems become visible through the people required to operate them. Section 9 may be elite, but it still exists inside a state whose interests are not automatically just.
Shirow’s Humor Is Part of the Argument

One of the adaptation’s most significant choices is its willingness to preserve humor. That may seem secondary beside the franchise’s themes of consciousness and cybernetic identity, but it is essential to Shirow’s worldview.

Humor prevents technology from becoming sacred. Characters can be brilliant and ridiculous in the same scene. Institutions can discuss national security while behaving like petty bureaucracies. Advanced machines can fail because someone misunderstood a human motive.

This tonal flexibility also protects Motoko from becoming a monument. She is not valuable because she represents an abstract “future human.” She is valuable because she is specifically herself: intelligent, flawed, amused, aggressive, and impossible to reduce to a philosophical symbol.

The manga’s humor also emphasizes embodiment. A cybernetic body may be replaceable, but it still has posture, appetite, awkwardness, and physical consequence. Comedy brings the body back into a story that could otherwise become purely cerebral.
Science SARU Is the Right Studio for This Version

Science SARU is an unusually strong match for Shirow’s manga because the studio is comfortable with tonal and visual contradiction. Its productions can be kinetic without losing character detail, and stylized without abandoning emotional seriousness.
Director Mokochan makes his series-directing debut after work on titles including
DAN DA DAN
Scott Pilgrim Takes Off
The Heike Story
, and
The Tatami Time Machine Blues
. Science-fiction author EnJoe Toh handles the script and series composition, while Shuhei Handa serves as character designer and executive animation director.
That combination suggests an adaptation built around movement and ideas in equal measure. EnJoe’s science-fiction background is particularly important.
Ghost in the Shell

requires a writer who can treat speculative concepts as systems rather than decoration. Handa’s designs, meanwhile, preserve the recognizable silhouettes of the franchise while moving closer to Shirow’s expressive manga style.
Science SARU’s work on
Jaadugar: A Witch in Mongolia
demonstrates how effectively the studio can turn thought, observation, and political intelligence into visual drama. Our analysis of
why knowledge is the most dangerous power in Jaadugar
examines that strength from a historical perspective.
Ghost in the Shell
applies a similar sensitivity to networks, bodies, and information.
A More Human Motoko Does Not Mean a Less Philosophical Series
Some viewers may interpret the new adaptation’s energy as a reduction in seriousness. That reaction is understandable because Oshii’s film established solemnity as the franchise’s prestige language.

But seriousness and slowness are not the same thing. A character can joke and still confront existential questions. A colorful world can still be politically oppressive. A fast-moving episode can still contain dense ideas about autonomy, labor, consciousness, and state power.

The new series’ real test is whether it can preserve complexity without imitating the emotional temperature of earlier adaptations. So far, its strongest choice is refusing to treat the 1995 film as the only legitimate model.
That does not diminish Oshii’s achievement. It restores the franchise’s range.
The Franchise Keeps Returning Because Its Questions Keep Evolving
Ghost in the Shell
has survived for decades because it is not built around one prediction of the future. Its core questions can be reinterpreted whenever technology changes the meaning of identity.

What counts as a body when prosthetics are superior to flesh? What counts as memory when memories can be edited? What counts as privacy when consciousness is networked? What counts as a person when intelligence can emerge without a biological birth?
The 2026 anime arrives at a moment when those questions no longer belong only to cyberpunk. They belong to everyday life.

Its return to Shirow’s manga is therefore not nostalgia. It is a strategic reset. By recovering the source’s humor, speed, visual density, and restless Motoko, Science SARU can ask old questions in a form that feels newly alive.
The strongest version of
The Ghost in the Shell
has never been the one that provides a final definition of humanity. It is the one that makes the definition unstable again.

children.text: The best K-dramas on Netflix right now include emotionally grounded series like
Move to Heaven
, critically acclaimed thrillers such as
The Glory
and
My Name
, beloved romances like
Crash Landing on You
and
Twenty-Five Twenty-One
, and breakout hits like
Extraordinary Attorney Woo
. These dramas offer exceptional storytelling, character depth, and emotional resonance over mere popularity.
Why Netflix Dominates K-Drama Streaming

Netflix has transformed from a K-drama distributor into the genre's most significant global platform. The streaming service invests in original productions, champions diverse storytelling, and makes Korean television accessible across 190 countries. This commitment has elevated K-dramas from niche interest to mainstream phenomenon, with shows regularly appearing in Netflix's global top 10.
While Netflix leads globally,
Prime Video has quietly built a strong catalog of character-driven Korean dramas
worth exploring as well.
Essential K-Dramas: Quality Over Hype
For Emotional Depth

body.alt: Move to Heaven Netflix K-drama emotional storytelling scene

children.text: Move to Heaven

remains one of Netflix's quietest masterpieces. The series follows trauma cleaners who sort through the belongings of the deceased, uncovering stories of lives lived in solitude and unexpected joy. Each episode functions as a standalone meditation on mortality and connection, anchored by the relationship between a young man on the autism spectrum and his ex-convict uncle. Watch this if you appreciate shows that trust silence as much as dialogue.

body.alt: My Mister Netflix K-drama quiet emotional drama scene

children.text: My Mister

examines the friendship between a middle-aged engineer drowning in quiet desperation and a young woman crushed by debt. The show refuses romance where other dramas would force it, instead presenting two people who become each other's reason to survive. The pacing is deliberate, the tone melancholic, but witnessing two damaged people slowly learn to breathe again is profoundly moving.
If stories about time passing and quiet regret resonate with you,
Reply 1988
explores growing up with even more restraint and emotional honesty.
For Thriller Enthusiasts

body.alt: The Glory Netflix K-drama revenge thriller main characters

children.text: The Glory

works because it understands that revenge is patient. The protagonist doesn't want quick violence—she wants her former bullies to understand exactly what they destroyed. Writer Kim Eun-sook crafts a narrative that's part psychological thriller, part indictment of class privilege, with Song Hye-kyo delivering a performance of controlled fury.

body.alt: My Name Netflix K-drama action revenge series scene

children.text: My Name

strips revenge down to its brutal essentials. A woman infiltrates the criminal underworld to find her father's killer, and the show commits fully to the physical and emotional toll of that journey. The action choreography is visceral, but what lingers is Han So-hee's portrayal of someone who has weaponized grief into something dangerous.
Best Romantic Korean Drama on Netflix

body.alt: Crash Landing on You Netflix K-drama romantic moment

children.text: Crash Landing on You

became a global phenomenon through earned emotion. The premise—South Korean heiress accidentally paraglides into North Korea and falls for a military officer—could have been pure fantasy. Instead, the show explores division, loss, and the small ways people build connection across impossible distances. The romance works because both leads are fully realized people before they're lovers.

body.alt: Twenty-Five Twenty-One Netflix K-drama youth romance scene

children.text: Twenty-Five Twenty-One

understands that first love doesn't require a happy ending to matter. Set against the 1997 Asian financial crisis, it follows two young people falling in love as their futures collapse. The show's bittersweet tone and refusal to provide easy answers make it more honest than most romance dramas.

body.alt: Business Proposal Netflix K-drama romantic comedy scene

children.text: Business Proposal

offers pure, self-aware romantic comedy. It knows exactly what it is—a contract-dating farce with attractive leads and absurd misunderstandings—and executes that vision with charm and energy. Sometimes you need a show that's simply fun.
For Unique Perspectives

body.alt: Extraordinary Attorney Woo Netflix K-drama courtroom scene

children.text: Extraordinary Attorney Woo

succeeded globally because it treated its protagonist's autism with specificity and respect. Woo Young-woo isn't a savant stereotype—she's a brilliant lawyer whose neurodivergence shapes how she sees the world and solves cases. The show balances legal drama, gentle humor, and genuine emotion without losing sight of its central character's humanity.

body.alt: Vincenzo Netflix K-drama mafia legal thriller scene

children.text: Vincenzo

shouldn't work—Italian-Korean mafia lawyer fights corrupt corporations using criminal methods in a show that can't decide if it's dark comedy, legal thriller, or action series. That tonal chaos becomes its strength. Song Joong-ki plays the lead with sardonic charm while the show embraces its absurdity while delivering genuine thrills.
Most Watched Korean Drama on Netflix
While popularity doesn't equal quality, some shows achieve both.
Squid Game
remains Netflix's most-watched non-English series globally.
All of Us Are Dead
Extraordinary Attorney Woo
, and
The Glory
have all ranked in Netflix's global top 10, proving diverse genres can find mainstream success.

body.alt: Queen of Tears Netflix K-drama emotional couple scene

children.text: Queen of Tears

became one of Netflix's most-watched K-dramas in 2024, breaking viewership records by subverting the typical chaebol romance formula. Instead of beginning with the meet-cute, it starts with a marriage falling apart, then asks whether two people can rediscover each other after years of resentment.
Recent Must-Watch Additions

body.alt: When Life Gives You Tangerines Netflix period K-drama scene

children.text: When Life Gives You Tangerines

has generated significant word-of-mouth for its 1950s period setting and emotionally grounded romance. Set on Jeju Island, it uses its historical backdrop to explore class, tradition, and personal agency in a rapidly changing Korea.

body.alt: Study Group Netflix Korean school action drama scene

children.text: Study Group

offers something different: a high school action-comedy about a brilliant student navigating a dangerous technical school, blending teenage drama with sharp social commentary about education and survival.

Who Should Watch What
New to K-drama?
Start with
Crash Landing on You
or
Extraordinary Attorney Woo
—both are accessible entry points that showcase what makes the medium special.
Want emotional catharsis?

, and

will make you feel things deeply.
Need escapist romance?

, and the lighter episodes of

Prefer dark, mature storytelling?

, and

offer complex moral landscapes and morally ambiguous protagonists.
For a more grounded, physical take on violence and loyalty,

Seeking something different?

(fantasy),

(horror), or

18 Rated Korean Drama on Netflix
For viewers seeking mature content, Netflix offers shows with more explicit material than traditional Korean broadcast television allows.

, and

contain graphic violence.
Nevertheless
and select romance dramas include more mature romantic content, though Korean entertainment generally remains conservative compared to Western standards.
Best Korean Series on Netflix: Hindi and Regional Options
For viewers in India seeking Hindi-dubbed versions, Netflix has expanded its K-drama dubbing efforts. Shows like
Crash Landing on You

Currently airing shows like

The Takeaway for New Viewers

The best K-drama on Netflix isn't the one with the highest viewership—it's the one that meets you where you are emotionally. Korean television has mastered the art of genre-blending and emotional specificity, creating shows that feel both universally human and culturally specific.

Start with whatever premise intrigues you. A courtroom drama about an autistic lawyer. A zombie outbreak in a high school. A woman plotting revenge across decades. Two people from divided countries falling in love. K-drama's strength is its range—there's room for fantasy epics and quiet character studies, broad comedy and devastating tragedy.

Netflix's catalog changes constantly. Shows arrive and depart, regional libraries differ, and what's trending shifts weekly. But the dramas listed here represent more than algorithmic popularity—they're entry points into a storytelling tradition that values emotional honesty, narrative ambition, and the belief that television can make you feel deeply.
Choose based on mood, not metrics. The right K-drama isn't the most-watched—it's the one that stays with you after the final episode ends.
